speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: UNITED GRAIN GROWERS LIMITED
speechtext: Before this bill is given first reading the hon. member should give us some information about it.

subtopic: UNITED GRAIN GROWERS LIMITED
speechtext:
The best explanation I could give would be by reading the general explanatory note as it appears in the bill:
The main purpose of the bill is to permit the equitable operation of the principle which has governed the company since its inception, namely, the principle that its business should be controlled by farmers actually engaged in farming. By 1911, chapter 80, by which the company was incorporated, only "farmers or owners or lessees of farms and the wives of such persons" were eligible to hold shares in the company otherwise than in cases authorized by a two-thirds vote at a shareholders' meeting (section 6); no shareholder was entitled to hold more than forty shares (section 5); and each shareholder had only one vote no matter how many shares stood in his name (section 8). The limitation on the number of shares a shareholder might hold was increased to one hundred by 1917, chapter 79, section 4, and by the same statute power was given to the company to substitute for a general shareholders' meeting a meeting of delegates chosen by local groups of shareholders, each delegate being entitled to one vote (section 6). Apart, however, from the exceptional cases provided for in section 6 of 1911, chapter 80, no transfer of shares held by farmers and their wives can be made to non-farmers. This restriction on transfers has seriously affected the value of shares belonging to farmers who have died or have ceased during their lives to be actually engaged in farming. The result has been an increasing proportion of the total capital of the company in fact the property of non-farmers whether registered as owners of the shares or not and consequently of persons who are not entitled to take part in the direction of the business of the company.
The provisions of the bill are chiefly directed to the correction of the situation thus created by permitting the creation of two classes of shares, one in the nature of preference shares on the ownership of which there is no occupational limitation but which do not entitle the holders to take part in the management of the company, and the other in the nature of common shares capable of being held only by farmers and carrying the right to take part in the election of delegates and to act as delegates.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext:
Two days ago, as well as on a previous occasion, the hon. member tor Broadview (Mr. Church) made inquiry as to the advisability of getting the census information sheets into individual hands prior to the enumerators making their rounds. I consulted the census authorities on this, and they advise me that it would not be practicable because it would mean that the enumerators would have to go over the whole ground twice and quite probably the questions would not be properly answered when they got the forms back. I am informed also that only four or five of the questions on the population schedule might cause any difficulty. These deal with racial origin, nationality and occupation. Copies of the forms covering the population schedule can easily be made available to any who desire them.
Ten years ago some 800,000 forms were sent out to farmers some weeks ahead, but my officials say that this did not help at all and the enumerators had to do the full work when they reached the farms. Forms have already gone out with the advertisements to all the newspapers, but our officials say that it is up to the newspapers to decide whether or not they will publish the questions. Some have done so already. In connection with advertising the schedules, our officials state that this would be difficult and very expensive, considering the fact that all our advertising has gone out. They point out also that without lengthy explanation, the mere printing of the questions would not be very helpful.

When, the
house adjourned yesterday the minister had promised to take 'this resolution under consideration with a view to considering the advisability of granting exemption from the tax on gasoline to primary producers. Has he given further consideration to the matter, and if so what decision has he arrived at?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) :
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last night I
promised that I would bring to the attention of my colleagues the remarks of the leader of the opposition. I did so, and the matter has been considered again, but I have to inform the committee that for the reasons I have stated on several occasions since the resolution came before the committee, the government does not feel that it would be justified in providing for a refund or making provision for exemption, of any class in the community.
I do not know that I can add anything to what I have said before. It is admitted that there are arguments on both sides. All I can say is that the government is strongly of the opinion that the arguments for no exemption or refund are stronger than the opposing arguments.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is it not true that all the provinces have some system either of refunds or of selling gas of a different colour to farmers for power purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I believe they do.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
All of
them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I believe so.

Both the
minister and some of the members who have voiced objection in the past few days to granting this exemption to primary producers seem to be under the misapprehension that we are asking for some special concession. The thing we have been trying to convey to the committee is that the principle of granting exemption from taxation to producers in respect of commodities used in their production is a principle which the government itself has recognized in practically all its taxation. A number of examples might be cited.
We pointed out the other day in connection with the use of electricity that the eight per cent tax which applies all over Canada, even in districts where electricity costs as much as twelve cents per kilowatt, is not imposed on industries which can show that the electricity is used for the production of their commodities. In that case they are exempt. This government almost every day in the year is rebating large amounts of money to manufacturers in respect of sales tax paid by them on materials used in their production.

I understand that even in the imposition of this gasoline tax the government proposes to allow the provincial governments and the employees of provincial governments to get their gasoline tax free. In other words, in Saskatchewan, for instance, where the farmer will have to pay three cents a gallon more for the gasoline he requires in order to carry on his farming operations, the provincial government inspector driving down the road will not have to pay the three cents a gallon tax, if I understood correctly the minister's statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Just a minute. There is no personal exemption to any employee of the provincial government. It has been a well settled principle of all our tax legislation that the dominion government does not impose taxes on provincial governments, which in turn would have to raise those taxes from their people through provincial taxation measures. It is only on sales to his majesty in the right of the province that there has been an exemption from the sales tax and excise taxes. I think there should be a similar exemption in this legislation. But that is a different thing from granting a personal exemption to an employee of a provincial government.

The minister will understand that I am referring to an inspector using gasoline not for his personal purposes but in carrying out his governmental duties. If I understood correctly the minister's statement the other evening, gasoline purchased by the government of Saskatchewan for use by its employees will be tax free. Is that not so?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is my intention that the section now in the Excise Tax Act shall apply to a transaction of the kind. If we departed from that principle we would be inviting strong, and as I look at the matter now, justifiable protests from all provincial governments. See what it might lead to. If the dominion government imposed taxes on his majesty in the right of the province, the incidence of which fell on the taxpayers of the province, it would mean that we would be taking or could take an advantage there which certainly would not be regarded as justifiable.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I have the floor for a moment? I have given a good deal of consideration to this problem-

Mr. Chairman, I protest. The hon. member for Weyburn was on his feet and sat down only when the Minister of Finance rose to make an interjection.

I did not appreciate the fact that the hon. member for Weyburn had the floor, otherwise I certainly would not have risen. May I say briefly what I intended to say? In regard to the question of taxation by the crown in the right of the dominion on the crown in the right of the province, I believe there is a legal difficulty. I have not prepared any brief in the matter, but has the minister or have the officials of his department at any time considered this aspect of the question, whether there is the right to tax the crown in the right of the province? It has given me some difficulty. I doubt very much if there is the legal right of taxation by the crown in the right of the dominion on the crown in the right of the province. If the minister has any opinion on the point, I should like to have it made clear.
Before I sit down, may I thank the hon. member for Weyburn.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have no reasoned opinion
to express on the legal point raised. All I know is that we do it right along. The crown in the right of the province pays customs duties imposed by this parliament, and which have been imposed upon them, I suppose, ever since confederation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Then, if
I may be permitted the observation at this point, the argument which the minister has advanced against the contention of the hon. member for Weyburn falls to the ground. You impose customs duties, and the money comes from the taxpayers of the provinces through their treasury. You refuse to tax them on gasoline because of the reasons alleged, and it will come out of exactly the same people. The minister's position is inconsistent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is only superficially inconsistent. The general purpose of the customs tariff is protective.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is protective.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
And this
from my hon. friend from Nova Scotia!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not expressing any
views on the theory. I am merely stating a matter of fact. We have a protective tariff in this country. Nobody has denied that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I agreeand the highest we have ever had in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is another point; I do not want to start an argument on it. I am simply saying that, in a purely revenue measure, where the sole object is the raising of taxes, I believe it has always been a principle of the legislation not to impose a tax on a province.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
With
great respect to the minister, it seems to me that that is a distinction without a difference, and one which will not carry conviction to the people of this country.

The point that I was starting out to make was that those of us who were asking for the exemption of farmers and fishermen from this gasoline tax were not demanding any concession; we were merely requesting the government to apply a principle which it has recognized in its taxation measures, which it recognized in the electricity tax, which it recognizes every year in the sales tax, and which the minister himself has said it is now going to recognize in the application of this tax with reference to the provincial governments. I am not quarrelling with that attitude, but I am pointing out that the provincial governments and their employees enjoy rebates or at least have tax-free gasoline in respect of this particular impost. Now, this committee has no assurance that there will not be abuses under those conditions. We have no guarantee that provincial government employees will
Special War Revenue Act

not use tax-free gasoline for their private purposes. The people are going to know that inspectors driving provincial government cars are using tax-free gasoline, while they themselves have to pay a tax of three cents a gallon on the same kind of gasoline when they use it in carrying on their farming operations.
The Minister of Finance is not very familiar with the situation on the prairies, but I can tell him that in Saskatchewan one of the things we have more than anything else is inspectors. As a matter of fact if in looking for a source of revenue he put a tax on inspectors he could raise a considerable sum. I do not know whether it would be wiser to ask them to buy a licence plate each year, or put a tax on the farmers and have an open season on inspectors like a duck shoot.
Are they mostly political heelers?

I would not say that all of them are political heelers, but a good many of them certainly find it difficult to differentiate between their government duties and their political duties. In my own constituency, throughout the political campaign last year, a government inspector driving a government car attended almost every meeting I held, and had a shorthand reporter with him to take down my speeches. I do not know whether he was using government gasoline.
Perhaps he was one of the hon. member's supporters.

I am afraid not. He was working, I believe, for the Minister of Agriculture.
The point I am making is that the government has already granted exemptions, so that the danger of abuse, if any there be, has already arisen. The minister is not on very good ground in saying, when we ask that the same principle be applied to the primary producers, that his only reason for not granting what he admits to be a just exemption is that there will be-to use his own words- wholesale evasion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, that is not the only reason.

The minister gave that the other night as his main reason- that there would be wholesale evasion. Personally I do not take that kindly. I do not believe the people throughout Canada will take it very kindly. The industrialist is exempt on his electricity tax. That must mean that the minister is not afraid he will cheat.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No danger.
The manufacturer is to be given a rebate. Presumably there is no danger of his cheating.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Practically none.
The provincial civil servants also enjoy exemption. Apparently there is no danger there.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Very little.

But the farmer and the fisherman, who are going to use this fuel to produce goods which this country needs in time of war, are not to be granted any exemption, because they are not trustworthy, because the minister thinks they are going to evade the tax and illegally use gasoline. It is discriminatory legislation; it is a discriminatory tax. I do not believe that the farming or fishing population will take it very kindly; they will look upon it as a reflection on their honour.
The other evening the minister asserted that in one province where purple gas is used there have been as many as one to two hundred convictions a month. The only province in which purple gas has been used over any period of time is Saskatchewan, so that the minister could not have referred to any other province. All the information I can obtain- and the same thing was said yesterday by the hon. member for Rosthern-is that the figure the minister gave is very high. In my opinion it is incorrect. The hon. member for Rosthern said yesterday that there had been in the neighbourhood of thirty convictions a month.
Why does the hon. gentleman say the statement is incorrect?

Because the information I get through talking to policemen and men engaged in legal work is that the number of court cases for evasion of the provincial gasoline tax has been comparatively small. I will say more. Saskatchewan was the pioneer in using purple gas as a means of preventing the abuses of the provision exempting gas used by farmers for productive purposes. After they had tried it for, I believe, some two years, the neighbouring province of Alberta sent its officials into Saskatchewan to study the Saskatchewan system. My information is that they were so much pleased with it and felt that it worked so efficiently that they went back and recommended its adoption, and Alberta has now launched upon the coloured gas system of preventing evasion of the gasoline tax levy. It seems to me, therefore, that the minister is allowing some people who are advising him to convince him

Special War Revenue Act
that this problem would present larger administrative difficulties than, I am sure, are likely to arise.
I am sure that if he consulted the government of Saskatchewan, or the Minister of Agriculture who comes from Saskatchewan, or any of the other members from that province, he would be told that in the main the farming population there have appreciated the fact that they have been given gasoline for productive purposes free of gasoline tax, and that any man in the community who tries to evade it is not looked upon as smart, but simply as doing something which, if he is allowed to continue to do it, will work to the injury of the rest. I know one or two men who have been convicted, and I can assure the committee that they are looked upon with great disfavour by their fellow farmers. The average man there would rather be caught horse stealing than be caught using purple gas in his car, not only because of the legal penalty but because of the social disapproval with which he is met in the community for doing something that is harmful to the standards of the entire farming group to which he belongs.
The minister is not on good ground when he says that his only reason for refusing to exempt the primary producers from the gasoline tax is his fear that they will cheat. That statement is not warranted. The government, if it wanted to do so, could devise the necessary system for exempting farmers and fishermen and at the same time prevent any large-scale evasion.
Yesterday a number of amendments were moved and were ruled out of order. The chairman did say, however, that it might be possible to move an amendment which would be in order. Without seeking to put myself in the class of hon. members who were referred to yesterday by the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) as trying to make heroes of themselves, I wish to offer an amendment for the consideration of the committee. I am sorry that the minister himself, in consequence of his consideration of the matter, did not bring in an amendment. I felt certain, when the committee rose yesterday at six o'clock, that such an amendment would be introduced, thus obviating the necessity for private members proposing amendments. I therefore wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright):
That resolution 6 of the Special War Revenue Act be amended by adding the following words:
Provided always that a rebate of the full amount of the tax paid by any farmer or fisherman shall be made upon satisfactory proof that the gasoline upon which the tax was paid
was utilized by such farmer or fisherman exclusively for power purposes upon his farm or in his fishing boat, and in lieu thereof that the eneral tax on gasoline shall be increased to a gure sufficient to compensate the treasury for the amount lost by reason of the proposed rebate.
I would point out that I am not proposing a new tax. I am adhering to that clause in standing order 60, section 552, which reads:
. . . these proposals must be grafted upon the financial scheme submitted by the government, and must not affect the balance oi ways and means voted for the service of the year.
In other words, we feel that the people who are driving cars for pleasure could afford to pay enough, in addition to this three cents, to compensate the treasury for what it would lose by exempting farmers and fishermen from payment of the tax. It is not my wish to embarrass the minister or to hold a gun at his head, and if he is prepared to reconsider this whole matter and let it stand I will willingly withdraw the amendment. I do think, however, that the government has brought down this proposal without giving it thorough consideration. Some of the gentlemen opposite who say "Oh, oh" forget that yesterday almost every member who stood up and pleaded with the minister for exemption from the tax for farmers and fishermen was a supporter of the government. I would remind hon. members who say "Oh, oh" that almost every member who has spoken, from west of the great lakes, and some from eastern Canada, have pleaded with the minister along the lines of my present submission.

We are a Liberal
party.

You are a Liberal party. Surely, then, it is not too much to appeal to the members of this committee to place the interests of their constituents above party adherence. After all, the function of parliament is to make known to the executive how any piece of legislation will affect the rank and file of the people. That is what we are here for. It has been made known by every group in the house that the imposition of this tax on the primary producers will be looked upon by them as unjust and unfair. If as a result of representations by private members, the minister were to change this tax so as to provide for exemption, it would be looked upon not as a defeat for him but as a victory for democracy. That sort of thing could not happen in Germany and Italy, and unfortunately it happens all too seldom in Canada that members stand up against something which they think will hurt
Special War Revenue Act

their constituents even though they believe it means coming into conflict with the party whip. Unless we are prepared to do as members have done in the past few days, who have opposed their own party and the government, we shall be doing a great disservice to democracy and to those parliamentary institutions for which we profess to be waging a war.
The hon. gentleman who has just sat down-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before dealing with this amendment, I must express regret if my words of yesterday were taken as an encouragement to present amendments. I simply had in mind the well known rule which is to be found in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms:
108. The Speaker decides the questions of order only when they actually arise and not in anticipation.
When an hon. member suggested that no amendment would be considered, I simply drew the attention of the committee to that rule. The amendment now proposed has, in large part, the characteristics of those submitted yesterday, and in particular it infringes upon the well-known rule that no increase may be considered in either an existing or a new or temporary tax for the service of the year except upon the initiative of a minister acting on behalf of the crown. The proposed amendment, in providing that the compensation shall be made by an increase in the gasoline tax on other classes of consumers, is directly in opposition to the rule just referred to. I must therefore rule the amendment out of order.
Before you give your ruling, Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: My ruling has been given.
You did not give us an opportunity to speak.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is the duty of the Chair or the Speaker to rule a motion out of order when the occasion arises. But an appeal can be taken from the ruling of the Chair.

Yesterday you told us that
while you would give your decision if you took the point as your own, when it was raised by the minister you would afford hon. members the opportunity to give their views. That is a time-honoured practice. Then having given your decision it should be adhered to. We have not been given an opportunity, and I have a point that I should like to submit for your consideration.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have no objection
to giving any hon. member an opportunity to speak, but I recall that yesterday I drew a distinction. When a point of order is raised by a member of the committee, opportunity is given to all hon. members to speak to the point of order. But the position is different when the procedure submitted is ruled out of order by the Chair or the Speaker. When there is no point of order raised, the chairman rules the procedure in question out of order on his own motion. But in deference to hon. members of the committee I have no objection to advising the committee that I am about to render a ruling, and if any hon. member desires to speak I shall be pleased to hear him.

I thank the chairman and
the committee for permission to speak. I would observe that it is a custom-possibly not the fixed rule-for the chairman not to rule on a point of order until one is raised; then he gives his ruling. However let that go.
The adverse ruling that has been given is based on citation 552 on page 164.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Citation 555.

Well, 552 seems to have
more bearing. Yesterday when the Minister of Finance raised the point of order he did it under 552. While his point of order was well taken on that occasion, he cannot well take advantage of the same rule to obtain an opposite ruling. I point out that I think the chairman contradicted himself in the ruling he gave yesterday. Citation 552 says:
Though it is the function of the committee of ways and means to impose rather than to repeal taxes, examples of the repeal of taxation effected in this committee are to be found upon the journals.
Then it goes on to say:
Proposals for the variation or modification of taxation can therefore be made in the committee;

That, I submit, is exactly what the hon. member for Weyburn has done; he has made a proposal for the variation of a tax submitted by the Minister of Finance. It goes on to say:
-but these proposals must be grafted upon-
That is an unhappy word.
-the financial scheme submitted by the government.
In other words it must be in accord with the scheme submitted by the government. You could not say that in substitution for a tax on gasoline you would put a tax on goats. It must accord with the general scheme submitted by the government-and must not affect the balance of ways and means voted for the service of the year.

Special War Revenue Act
On that point, too, the proposal of the hon. member agrees; it is in accordance with the general scheme submitted by the government, which is taxation on gasoline. As to affecting the balance of ways and means voted for the service of the year, this is not a question of voting money for the service of the year at all, and the whole thing might be thrown out in that regard. The proposal of the hon. member for Weyburn does not affect the total because he proposes only a substitution.
Amendments, therefore, can be proposed to substitute another tax, or equivalent amount,-
The hon. member proposes another tax of equivalent amount for that proposed by the government.

as, for instance, a proposal to substitute probate and legacy duty on real property as an alternative for an inhabited house duty.
The crown in one case wanted to impose a tax on house property, and the alternative was to suggest probate and legacy duty. I point out that the proposed substitute is not one of dollars and cents but of a system. They propose a tax in this form as against a tax in that form. It was argued by the Chairman yesterday that because the exact amount was not given-it certainly could not be given-the amendment was out of order. The clear intention is that as long as the alternative method is submitted, it is up to the government to arrange the other proposed taxation in terms that will produce the same amount. But an alternative method can be submitted. Therefore I suggest that it is in order, that the hon. member complies with all those conditions. He proposes a modification of the taxation; he drafts his proposal on the same kind of taxation, the same method of taxation, namely, a tax on gasoline. He only changes to a comparatively small amount what may be called the incidence of the tax. He puts it on Jones, Smith and Brown, makes them pay a little more, and leaves it off Johnston. He does not affect the total balance at all; he says the equivalent shall be made up. If I had been drawing the amendment, instead of using the words "decrease" or "increase" I should have used the words "change"; and I think that would have met the Chairman's objection, because he is going to say under section 555 that you cannot increase a tax. But we will not say anything about increasing or decreasing; we do not know. We simply say that we will substitute one method for the other, and if there is any change in amount we will make the change to coordinate with the previous amount.
The Chairman says that under paragraph 555-
-no increase can be considered either of an existing or of a new or temporary tax for the service of the year, except on the initiative of a minister acting on behalf of the crown.
The hon. member is not suggesting a new tax at all; he is doing exactly what 552 says he can do-proposing a substitute. If he proposed a tax on horseshoes, that would be a new tax and would not be permissible unless moved by a member of the administration. But 552 is not to be mixed up with 555. Paragraph 555 refers to an individual attempt by a member to put on a new tax; that is illegal. The minister himself quoted 552, and he cannot very well ignore it now. He had the advantage of it yesterday, and properly so, I think, but he ought to accept it to-day.
I submit the amendment is in order because it complies in every respect with the definite specifications laid down by 555.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Does any other hon. member desire to speak to the point of order?
The rule is well known that no increase can be considered either of an existing or a new or temporary tax for the service of the year except on the initiative of a minister acting on behalf of the crown. The amendment purports to increase the tax in its incidence upon other classes of taxpayers. I must rule, therefore, that, the effect of the amendment being to increase the burden on the taxpayer, the amendment is out of order as ultra vires of a private member.
In May, 13th edition, page 511, I find the following:
The principle that the sanction of the crown must be given to every grant of money drawn from the public revenue, applies equally to the taxation levied to provide that revenue. No motion can therefore be made to impose a tax, save by a minister of the crown, unless such tax be in substitution, by way of equivalent, for taxation at that moment submitted to the consideration of parliament; nor can the amount of a tax proposed on behalf of the crown be augmented, nor any alteration made in the area of imposition.
That is from May, a recognized authority on parliamentary procedure.
I submit, sir, that May is resorted to only when Beauchesne does not deal with the point in question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There is a remedy that lies with the committee; that is, an appeal to the house. The other day one hon. member suggested that the Chairman or the Speaker was above everyone else within this house. I should like to state my conception
Special War Revenue Act

of the duty of the Speaker or the Chairman. It is clearly set out in paragraph 104 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms:
The presiding officer, though entitled on all occasions to be treated with the greatest attention and respect by the individual members, because the power, and dignity, and honour of the assembly are officially embodied in his person, is yet but the servant of the house.
After a ruling has been given an appeal may be taken to the house.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
On the main motion
which is before the committee-
Just a moment; I want to appeal that ruling.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am not speaking to the point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is no point of order.
But I want to appeal from that ruling, as I am entitled to do.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Very well, if you will make the motion.

I am making it.
Mr. Speaker resumed the chair, and the Chairman of the committee made the following report:
When resolution No. 6, Special War Revenue Act amendment, was under consideration in committee of ways and means, Mr. Douglas (Weyburn) moved:
"Provided always that a rebate of the full amount of the tax paid by any farmer or fisherman shall be made upon satisfactory proof that the gasoline upon which the tax was paid was utilized by such farmer or fisherman exclusively for power purposes upon his farm or in his fishing boat, and in lieu thereof that the general tax on gasoline shall be increased to a figure sufficient to compensate the treasury for the amount lost by reason of the proposed rebate."
The Chairman ruled this amendment out of order on the ground that it would increase the proposed tax, and that it was not moved by a minister of the crown. Whereupon Mr. Neill appealed from the ruling of the Chairman.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I was paired with the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson). Had I voted I should have voted to support the ruling of the Chairman of the committee. I might say, in stating my position, that I assume the leader of the opposition would have been opposed to the ruling of the Chair.
And the house having resumed in committee of ways and means:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall resolution 6
carry?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution
has been before the committee now for some hours, and once or twice during the debate it has been suggested that the Minister of Agriculture should have been consulted or should have said something on the resolution. The hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas), speaking a few moments ago, suggested that if the Minister of Finance had consulted the government of Saskatchewan he would have received certain information, and that if he did not care to consult the government of Saskatchewan he might have consulted the Minister of Agriculture and received the information.
The information with regard to the number of prosecutions which have taken place in Saskatchewan in relation to the use of coloured gas is contained dn a wire which was sent from Regina yesterday. It is to this effect, that in 1939 there were 123 prosecutions for wrongful use of purple gas-1939 was the year in which the coloured gas was first used. In 1940 there were 618 prosecutions.
That is not 200 a month.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: In 1941, 58 prosecutions. "Approximate number of licences for trucks and cars, 125,000. Approximate number of farmers, 142,000. Experience in the use of purple gas very satisfactory." That is the complete information so far as Saskatchewan is concerned. I understand that the other day the Minister of Finance made the statement that it was reported to him by a member of a provincial government, not a member of the Saskatchewan government-
One of those using purple gas.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
-that in one province where the purple gas is used, from one to two hundred prosecutions a month have been made. But he did not say, monthly throughout the year. It is quite possible, and I would say quite probable, that in Saskatchewan, where cars in any considerable numbers are operated only during the six or seven summer
months, there may have been prosecutions running to the numbers which were stated by the member of a provincial government. But in any case the prosecutions in the only full year for which we have statistics were over six hundred, or over fifty per month for a twelve-month year-and we do not, of course, operate any considerable number of cars during the winter months in Saskatchewan in rural districts where coloured gas would be used. I suggest that the figures used by the minister are not so far out as may have been indicated by some of the statements made.
But that is not the reason why I rose to speak at the moment. It was in order to deal with some of the other suggestions which have been made during the debate, relating more particularly to agriculture, and the use of gasoline in gas tractors on the farms, and the effect of this particular legislation upon tractor farming.
One would judge, listening to the discussion, that the method by which a tax was to be put into effect, if it were a federal tax as against a provincial tax, would have no bearing upon this question. But those of us who have had experience in imposing gasoline taxes in provinces know that we met great difficulty in doing so, because provincially a gasoline tax must be put on as a direct tax, whereas when it is imposed federally it can be imposed as an indirect tax. When a province puts the tax on as a direct tax, it must of necessity deal with the individuals who are using the gasoline, and for that reason and because of the very nature of the administration that must be set up, must provide machinery to enforce the tax. There is no additional administration required in a province to enforce the tax. Additional administrative machinery would be necessary in connection with the putting on of a federal tax.
It may be said in reply to that, "But the provincial set-up could be used in administering this particular tax." But the answer is, in connection with the war tax, which after all is put on for the purpose of obtaining revenue for the dominion treasury, the sharing in the cost of a system so costly as a provincial system must be is not a necessity; the tax can be put on through the indirect method much more simply and effectively, and at a lower cost through the federal government than through following the system which we have in the provinces. In other words, as I see it, it is not necessary for the federal government to follow through to personal and individual prosecutions, so long as we do not adopt a plan of allowing refunds or avoidance of the tax.

Special War Revenue Act
Irrespective, however, of the arguments with respect to farming and farmers, and the effect of the tax on farmers, if our object is to get as much as we can out of this tax for the purpose of financing the war, it is better to keep to a system which does not necessitate going down to individuals, either in the placing of the tax, or in the administration, or in order to determine whether individuals are carrying out the intent of the law.
May I ask the minister a question in that connection?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I wish the hon. member would allow me to continue until I have completed my remarks, and then, if there is any answer required, I shall be quite prepared to give it.
The second argument was that since we allow a drawback where the gasoline is purchased by a province, there is no reason why we should not allow it to farmers. Well, if one is discussing the question from a merely academic point of view there is perhaps much to be said for that argument. And something might be said in favour of not permitting the exemption even to provincial governments and to municipalities.
There is a lot to be said in favour of it.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
But whether one is in favour of or opposed to the idea, I do not think it is necessary to go quite as far as the hon. member for Weyburn did in presenting the argument. I do not believe it is necessary, in this committee or in this house, whenever matters are discussed with respect to farming in western Canada, or the western provincial governments, particularly the province of Saskatchewan, to drag in the suggestion that someone who is working for the provincial government may be working for a political party. It may be quite true that men who work for the provincial government attend political meetings in Saskatchewan. It may be just as true that hon. members of this house and persons who work for the federal government attend political meetings which are addressed by members of the government and other hon. members who support the government; but it is not necessary to have that kind of argument in a discussion of this kind. When the proper time arrives for the discussion of such questions we shall be prepared, as we always have been, to deal with them; at least, those of us who have been associated with government in Saskatchewan have always been prepared to deal with them. Probably some of the success which we have experienced is because of the

fact that we have dealt with them, and dealt with them particularly before the people of this country.
You mean, "politically".

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
But it is not necessary to deal with them in connection with this debate.
I come now to another matter which has been brought up in this- house from time to time. It has been made to appear, on the one hand, that this is a tax imposed on all the farmers of Canada as against the rest of the people, and, on the other, that there is here an issue between the farmers of the west and the farmers of the east. Well, it is neither the one nor the other. It is not a tax which is levied on all the farmers of western Canada as against all the other farmers in the dominion, nor is it one from which all the farmers would be exempt as against all the other people. It is a tax which, even as now proposed, is levied on a very small percentage of the farmers of Canada. From the point of view that it discriminates in favour of the larger group of farmers as against a small group, there might be some argument. But there is no basis for the argument that it discriminates, against farmers as a class and favours other classes.
In that connection may I say that the Minister of Finance did discuss this matter with the Minister of Agriculture. He also discussed it with every other member of the cabinet. It was fully considered in council. It was discussed, as the minister said yesterday or the day before, over many days, in fact over a number of weeks, and the conclusions reached were arrived at after full discussion. I may say in addition that there has not been a single argument produced by any member of this committee which was not advanced by some member of the government while those discussions were proceeding. Not always were those arguments presented by the Minister of Agriculture, as representative of agriculture, because governments do not proceed in that way, but rather by some member of the cabinet in the interests of all the people. Every argument which has been produced in this chamber on either side against this particular tax in its present form was raised in council, and, I believe, by the minister even outside council in discussing the matter with his own officials. It was considered fully, and action was taken after it had been thoroughly considered.
One of the facts apparent to all of us was contained in representations which were made to the Minister of Finance, and to myself as Minister of Agriculture, by persons who

Special War Revenue Act
assemble or sell in this country tractors of certain types. According to an estimate made by the people who produce and sell these tractors, which estimate is, I believe, reliable-
What kind of tractors?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It happened to be the Massey-Harris company which made the representations, but in presenting these figures they are not limiting themselves to any particular type of tractor. They say:
According to reliable estimates there are about 107,000 tractors in use on Canadian farms.
That is the information which this company has, and I presume it is approximately correct. The statement is that "according to reliable estimates there are about 107,000 tractors in use on Canadian farms, of which approximately 50,000 are of the type designed for burning distillate or kerosene." These obviously are not affected by this particular tax-that is, 50,000 out of 107,000, or almost fifty per cent-"and about 23,000 are low compression tractors suitable for burning 57 to 60 octane gasoline." Of course, it is quite possible that in these engines there might be burned some types of fuel oil which will not be affected by this tax. But presuming they all bum gasoline, there are 23,000 of them suitable for burning 57 to 60 octane gasoline, "while 34,000 are of more modern high compression models burning 68 to 70 octane gasoline. It will be noted that approximately one-third of the tractors now in use are of the high compression type." In other words, one could argue that it is not necessary for more than one-third of the number of farmers who are operating tractors on farms to subject themselves to this particular tax. If one assumed that the 57,000 engines were built to bum gasoline, that they were all going to bum it, one could say that only a little more than half of the number of engines that are used on farms in Canada are subject to this particular tax. But when one recalls that there are about 750,000 farmers in Canada; when one remembers that there are 107,000 tractors; when one knows the situation that exists to-day and remembers that on farm after farm in the west where engines are used, more than one engine is in use, one will be convinced, I believe, that after all we are speaking only for a very small percentage of farmers when we are making all the noise that we have been making with regard to tractors.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
An hon. member says,
"no." I admit at once that gasoline is used on farms which is not used in tractors, but
when we get into classification, we enter a much broader field than has been discussed on the floor of the house in the few hours that we have been dealing with this matter. If we are to exempt from this tax all gasoline used for any purpose whatsoever, on the farm, we get into many of the classifications that would carry us into business. For example, there are men who use trucks entirely in business in the delivery of goods to farms all over the eastern provinces. Men are delivering bread, their entire trade being with farmers; delivering groceries, their entire trade being with farmers; collecting produce, their entire trade being with farmers. When, therefore, you enter upon that argument you eliminate so much of the tax that as a war tax it is of very little use to the government in raising moneys for the particular purpose for which it is designed.
That brings me to this point, as regards the discussion that has been going on. I do not say that this discussion should not be carried on, but it should be weighed for what it is worth. It is a discussion which, in so far as it has been crystallized in the amendments that have been proposed, as it affects farmers, concerns itself largely with the use of gasoline in tractors upon farms; and the number of tractors involved is approximately 50,000. When we consider that there are 750,000 farmers in Canada, we see that it is a very small proportion of the farmers about whom we are speaking. That is why I stated yesterday, or at least implied in a remark I made, that it was hardly right to suggest that this tax hurts all the farmers of Canada or all the farmers of the west. There is a much larger percentage of farmers who do not use tractors at all than there is of those who use them; and when hon. gentlemen across the floor say that, because a man talks in favour of using horses on the farm as against tractors, he is back in the horse-and-buggy stage in relation to agriculture, then those hon. gentlemen are talking against the actual kind of agriculture that is carried on by the great majority of farmers throughout Canada, both east and west.
All these matters had to be weighed in considering what the government would finally do; but the argument which weighs more than any other with me as Minister of Agriculture and as a farmer is that this is a tax imposed for the purpose of raising revenues for the prosecution of the war. The kind of taxes that are being compared with it are those that were imposed for the purpose of financing the building of roads in the provinces. But there is no comparison between the two taxes, either as regards the reason for imposing them or as regards the incidence

Special War Revenue Act
of the tax as it should be imposed) upon the people of the country, or the method by which it will be levied.
In the provinces we have had a gasoline tax for the purpose of building roads and maintaining them, and every time we have imposed a tax we have argued that it should go on and that an amount of money should be spent out of the treasury of the province for the purpose for which the tax was imposed. In most of the provinces that has happened. In the long run-
That is not true.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It may not be true in actual dollars and cents expended, in some years, but over a long term of years I think it will be found that in most of the provinces the gasoline tax is eventually spent either in building roads or in paying interest on the amount of money that has gone into road building, which is a very large amount, and also for the maintenance of roads from day to day. In any event, the reason given for imposing the tax, and for the method by which it was imposed, was that the money thus collected was to be used for the building and maintenance of roads in the provinces.
The argument immediately arises-why should you make other people pay? Why should you make them pay the tax if they use gasoline somewhere off the road? As a result of that argument being used, methods have been found of allowing people who are not using gasoline for driving cars or trucks on the road to have such gasoline exempted from taxation. But let me repeat, that is not the reason for imposing this tax. This tax is imposed for the purpose of raising funds with which to prosecute the war, and it was considered by the government that the tax levied upon all the people of Canada who use gasoline, no matter for what purpose they use it, would produce most with the least expense of collection. Whether that is right or not is a question which can be and ought to be discussed; but to compare this particular tax with the taxes that are imposed in the provinces, and to say that, because the provinces have exempted farmers, therefore farmers should be exempted by the federal government, is carrying the argument one step too far.
Coming to the question whether this tax should be imposed on farmers, or whether there should be any tax on farmers, I think we shall all agree that the farmer does pay his share of taxation, whether this three-cent tax is imposed or not. I am not arguing the question from that point of view at all. A three-cent tax on gasoline does mean something to many farmers. It does not mean as much as some of us would seem to have

convinced ourselves that it does with regard to many farmers of certain types, but it does mean something to the farmer who uses gasoline in a tractor to have a three-cent tax imposed.
But I think I am in agreement with at least sixty per cent, and probably seventy-five per cent, of the membership of this house when I say there never has been introduced in this house a budget which was so completely a farmers' budget as the budget introduced by the present Minister of Finance. That is recognized by farmers all across Canada. While those of us who are farmers and who represent farmers might feel that we are performing a service in speaking in this house on behalf of the farmer and saying he should not have to pay this three-cent tax on gasoline, I can say advisedly that ninety per cent of farmers in this country-and probably I am low in that figure-upon whom the tax is levied because they use tractors, will pay this three-cent tax believing that they are joining with the remainder of the people of Canada, in so far as they use gasoline, in paying it, knowing that this tax is going entirely into a fund which is to be used for the purpose of properly prosecuting this war at the present time.
I do not agree.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Whether my hon. friend agrees or does not, he will agree that hon. members are down to ten per cent of the farmers when they are talking on behalf of the men who are going to have to pay the tax in connection with tractors.
No, we are not.
What percentage of grain farmers?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I am not prepared to say that; but I am prepared to point out that the number of farmers who are farming in the three western provinces approaches 300,000. If there are only 107,000 tractors in all Canada, as my friends of the Massey-Harris company say, and if, as my hon. friend knows, many of the wheat farmers who are operating tractors are operating more than one, he will realize that only a percentage of farmers in western Canada, certainly considerably less than half of them, are affected by the arguments he has been putting forward in this committee. With 107,000 tractors in all Canada and approximately 300,000 farmers in the three western provinces, when one realizes that many of them have more than one tractor, I would say it is a very small minority of the farmers of the west to whom

Special War Revenue Act
he is appealing when he is speaking with regard to this matter. I do not say that should change his argument, because if I did I would be agreeing that one of the suggestions made earlier in the debate was correct, namely, that hon. members have been talking to their constituents. After all, I do not think there is any hon. member who, in talking against this particular tax, is talking to a majority of his constituents. He will be talking to a minority.
That being the situation, I say the question probably is being and certainly ought to be considered absolutely on its merits, and the merit upon which I considered it as a member of the government and as Minister of Agriculture is that there is a choice in the matter. It is a choice that would take some time to bring it into effect so far as a certain limited number of farmers are concerned; that is, farmers can avoid this tax, not in a dishonest way but by the method in which they carry on their agriculture. They can avoid it to a degree on the farms where they have engines that will not bum anything but gasoline, provided they have supplementary power in the form of horse-power. They can avoid it in places where they are changing engines, and to that extent companies who are putting out engines that will not bum other forms of fuel might have some complaint. They can avoid it in other ways.
I would, however, suggest to the committee that I think we have taken altogether too much time on this question. We have discussed it until I think every phase of it is before the country. The minister has been absolutely fair in placing the points, even the worst side of the argument, before hon. members who represent agriculture and fishing constituencies. From the point of view of the agriculturist I am prepared to say that the kind of leadership which I was asked last night by the hon. member for Acadia to give to this house I am prepared to give and have given in what I have said now, and that leadership is to support the Minister of Finance to the limit in seeing to it that this legislation goes on the statute books, that the tax is collected, and when it is collected I am sure it will be put to good use.
I desire only a few moments to say something with respect to what the minister has just said; I am not going to take up as much time as the minister-

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The hon. member has already had much more time than I have taken.

The minister usually takes twenty-five minutes and ends by saying that we have taken too much time.
He bases his entire argument on the fact that this tax is being raised for war purposes, and that the farmers will pay it gladly because it is going to be used for those purposes. The minister knows and every hon. member knows that the farmers will pay anything which they think they justly ought to pay as their contribution toward Canada coming out of this war victorious. The objection that we have made is this. Other taxes are also collected by this government for the purpose of winning the war. The tax on electricity to which I have referred, brought in by this government as a war measure, the sales tax, and other taxes are imposed for the purpose of raising revenue to fight the war." In all of those taxes the government has recognized the principle that commodities which enter into the cost of production ought to be exempt from taxation. Irrespective of whether many or few farmers are affected-I am not going into an argument with respect to that-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Permit me to interrupt. There is no drawback of the duties or sales tax on machinery for use in industrial plants; there is no drawback of sales tax on gasoline for use by manufacturers in carrying on their businesses. The hon. gentleman is entirely wrong and loose in his statements about that being a principle of general application. It is true there is a drawback of duty on materials, and of sales tax-I am not sure of that-but the principle does not carry through to such commodities as machinery, plant, fuel and that kind of thing.

I am quite aware of what the minister has said, but the principle does apply to raw materials which certain manufacturers buy, which enter into their cost of production. We are not attempting to play off the farmer of the east against the farmer of the west or tractor farmers against horse farmers. The minister may be right that it affects a small number of farmers, although personally I do not agree with him; I think the figure is much larger than he computed.
The point is, here is a tax going to be placed upon what enters into the farmers' cost of production. The principle has been recognized in some other respects, as the minister has said, and we ask that it be recognized in this respect. The farmer's fuel is a large item in his cost of production, and if that fuel is taxed, his cost of production is increased by the amount of the tax. He is one of

the few producers in Canada who is not in a position to-day to pass on an increase in the cost of production. speechtext: May I say I was not replying all the time to my hon. friend. It was a remark made on the other side that led me to make that observation.

I am aware of that, but we of this group have never suggested anything of the kind. We have asked that the government should give consideration to granting tax exemptions on fuel actually used on the farm in farming operations.
I have only one other observation to make before I sit down, and I do not propose to press this matter further, since apparently the government is adamant with regard to it. The figures given by the Minister of Agriculture certainly do not bear out the statement made the other evening by the Minister of Finance. This afternoon we were told that in Saskatchewan there were 123 convictions in 1939, 618 in 1940, and 58 so far in 1941. That is a long way from the 100 to 200 a month mentioned by the Minister of Finance. That figure, in relation to the number of farmers in Saskatchewan who drive cars, represents about two-fifths of one per cent.
i Mr. ROSS (Moose Jaw): That does not necessarily represent anything like the total number of evasions; it may be only a very small percentage. That is only the number who were caught.

If the hon. member for Moose Jaw thinks there are many more evasions in Saskatchewan than there are convictions, he is saying one of two things: either that the Saskatchewan authorities have been slack in checking up on people who have been evading this tax, or that there are great numbers of people in that province who are crooked and not to be trusted. I would not want to accept either statement; the hon. member must assume responsibility for them.

In one year there were more than 600 convicted of evading the tax. No matter how many policemen you had looking into these matters, you could never catch all who were attempting to evade the law. My hon. friend knows that as well as I do; there must have been many more evasions than convictions.

I know nothing of the sort; I do not know that there were many more evasions. I only know that the highest figure was 618 convictions in 1940, which represents about two-fifths of one per cent of the total number of farmers with motor licences in Saskatchewan. That is infinitesimal.
The Minister of Agriculture raised one other point which he did not develop but which I think is worth considering. It was suggested that the federal government could use the machinery of the provincial governments in order to make these rebates. The minister merely said that would not do, and did not elaborate the point. Since, apparently, the government is not going to do anything in the way of rebates this year, perhaps the minister might consider, or set up a committee in his department to study, the various provincial systems, with a view to bringing in next year an amendment under which these exemptions may be granted. There is no reason why the provincial machinery should not be used, because the gasoline that is tax free under the provincial government is the same gasoline that would be tax free under the federal government. It would not be necessary to set up two police forces, or to have both provincial and federal machinery to bring evaders into court. A man caught using gasoline that was tax free might be automatically convicted under both federal and provincial statutes. The machinery of the federal and provincial governments could, I should imagine, be brought into harmony without any great difficulty.

It seems to me, however, that the government should have explored, and certainly should now explore, the possibility of using the provincial machinery in order that the federal government may grant to the farmers what it is now granting to other groups in Canada, namely, the right to obtain, without the payment of this tax, an item that enters into their

Special War Revenue Act
cost of production. When we ask that, I do not think we are asking anything unreasonable. The farmers are not seeking to be relieved from their share of the cost of financing the war; they are merely asking that they be relieved from an increase in the cost of an item which enters so greatly into their cost of production, which increase they cannot pass on to anyone else.

I did not intend to participate further in this discussion, and I can assure hon. members that I am not going to take very long now, since I am convinced that the government intends to adopt this measure without change, in spite of the protests that have been made from all sections of the chamber. I listened with particular attention to the arguments advanced by the Minister of Agriculture. If the truth were known, I believe he was arguing against his own convictions. I think he realizes as well as the rest of us that many of his arguments might be classified as sophistry and nothing else. I shall, however, give him the benefit of the doubt, but for just a few moments I should like to discuss two or three of the arguments he advanced.
The minister gave the number of convictions that have been registered in Saskatchewan. If my arithmetic is correct, these figures show that only about one-tenth of one per cent of the people of that province have been convicted of evading payment of this tax, and, after all, this is a very small percentage. I should like also to support the suggestion offered by the hon. member for Weyburn, namely, that the machinery already set up in the various provinces might be utilized by the federal government in order to refund this tax, if the government saw fit to make such refunds.
For a moment or two I should1 like to compare the statement made this afternoon by the Minister of Agriculture with something said yesterday by the Minister of Finance. Yesterday we were told that approximately one-sixth of this tax would have to be refunded if the government accepted the suggestion that farmers and fishermen should be given rebates in connection with gasoline used for power purposes on farms and in fishing boats. But the Minister of Agriculture told us only a few moments ago that less than ten per cent of all the farmers of this country are using tractors driven by gasoline. It seems to me that if one-sixth of this whole tax is to be borne by less than ten per cent of our farmers, a substantial burden will be imposed upon those few farmers who use gasoline as tractor fuel instead of carrying on their farming operations by other methods. The minister also stated that of the 107,000 farmers
in Canada who use tractors on their farms, only fifty per cent use gasoline as fuel. If that is so, it seems to me that this tax will bring about a decided discrimination in favour of those farmers who use other types of fuel. A good many farmers are using crude oil and other substitutes for gasoline, and I should like to ask just why the farmers who use gasoline should have to shoulder this burden, while farmers using other types of fuel are not. to be taxed. It seems to me most unfair and unreasonable that one section of one particular class should be discriminated against in this way. I was very much interested in the vote that just took place-

It seems to me strange, however, that so far I have heard nothing from representatives of industrial communities such as the one from which I come. I hope the time will come when this house will consider the broad, general principles of taxation and see if it is not possible to levy taxes in a less objectionable form than that which we now use. But that time has not come, and the methods of taxation which are now proposed are the traditional methods of this house. This is not the time to go into the broad, general principles involved. That time may come shortly, and when it does I shall have something to

say. In view of the methods that we have adopted, this tax is as little objectionable as any other that has been imposed against production, consumption, trade and so forth. No one will be able to hide behind this taxation and make money out of it, as can be said with regard to some of the other taxes which are levied.
I support this measure because it is a general measure that will apply to everybody. Listening to the debate, one would have fancied that this was a farmer's question. It strikes me that if the farmers of this country had been able to listen in to this debate, had been able to watch their own representatives ask that we make fish of one and tractors of another, they would have felt that they cut rather sorry figures before their own communities. This is a national tax for a national purpose. If they are to be given exemptions, then I shall ask for my own exemptions.
Exemptions are given now.

I suppose the hon. member means so far as the provincial governments are concerned. Perhaps that is taking it out of one pocket and putting it into another. I would not object if this tax was applied to the gasoline used by the provincial governments. I have not noticed any of the provincial governments exempting the federal government from taxation upon the gasoline it uses. It might be fish for one and flesh for the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is exempted.

Then I shall take that back. There is a good reason why we should make that exemption. Generally speaking, this is a national tax for a national purpose, levied upon all people in a like manner. If that is going to be changed, then I shall have an amendment to offer. I should like to see the little storekeeper in my riding-and there are many of them-exempted from paying the tax upon the gasoline he uses in the little car with which he makes deliveries. He will have to add this tax to the price of his commodities, and this will increase the cost of living of the poor people whom I represent. I should like to see the working man exempted from paying this tax upon the gasoline which he uses in the little car in which he rides to work. I think I could make out a very good case on his behalf. I should like to see the working man exempted from paying this tax upon the gasoline which he uses in the little Ford car in which he takes his wife and

Special War Revenue Act
family to the country to visit some of his farmer friends and thus get a little relief from the heat and hard work of the city.
I can make an argument for every class there is in Canada. Let us all be exempt and then we shall all be satisfied. If any exceptions are to be made to this tax, the whole thing may as well be abolished. I am ready to support it for one reason only, namely, that it is a tax of general application. If the Minister of Finance proposes to exempt the members of one community simply because of the noise that has been made on their behalf, then I shall make some noise. If he is going to exempt some classes and then place an increased tax upon the people whom I represent, then I shall say it is most unjust. I do not know whether I shall vote against it or not, but I do not think the minister will give me that chance. I would consider such a tax very unfair and unpatriotic. I am going to vote for this as a national tax, levied for a national purpose upon all citizens. Some of us are farmers; some, city people; some, lawyers and so on, but that is merely the way in which we make our living. Fundamentally we are neither farmers nor workers. Fundamentally in this assembly we are Canadians, and I am going to vote for this because it is Canadian, not because I like the fundamental principle but because it is the best we have before us.

Mr. Chairman, we have spent two or three days discussing this resolution to impose a tax on gasoline, and several hon. members have spoken in opposition to it, but I do not believe that this tax is nearly so serious as some of these hon. gentlemen have tried to make out. There are thirty-eight farmers in this house, and on the government side only one farmer member has spoken in opposition to this resolution. Those who have spoken against it have been mostly lawyers and businessmen, and the odd clergyman.
We represent the farmers as well as some of you farmer members do.

I sometimes wonder why certain members take such a tremendous interest in farmers' problems at certain times. I believe that the farmer members of this house are quite capable of looking after the interests of the farmers, and when any question comes up which vitally affects the fanner, these farmer members can be trusted to speak upon it.
I am a farmer and I run a tractor. I also represent one of the larger rural constituencies in Ontario, and so far I have not had one
protest from any farmer in my constituency against this tax. If there were any serious objections to it by the farmers, I feel quite certain that I should have heard from them, just as I do on other questions that affect their interests. After all, this is a small matter. The average farmer running a tractor will not use more than 300 gallons of gasoline in a season. The extra tax on that would be only $9, and, in any event, it will affect only a small percentage of our farmers. I feel quite certain that the farmers of my constituency are not objecting to this tax.

Has the minister taken into consideration the advisability of having equality of taxation on gasoline as between the maritime provinces and the rest of Canada? It seems most unfair to users of gasoline in the maritime provinces that they should have to pay a tax of thirteen cents a gallon, while in other parts of Canada the gasoline tax is very much less. This principle of equality was recognized by the minister in the income tax resolutions, and adjustments were made with the provinces so that the income tax payers would not have to pay double taxation. The minister relieved them to that extent. What representations have been made, or what has been done to bring about an equalization of gasoline taxes throughout Canada? Have any representations been made to the provincial governments that they might reduce their taxes as a contribution to the war effort and in order that users of gasoline in Nova Scotia and the maritime provinces might be put on a parity with gasoline users in other parts of Canada?
The principle has been enunciated in this house by the minister and by many others that taxation should be imposed according to the ability of the people to pay. If that principle is to be applied in the maritime provinces, the greatest consideration should be given to our farmers, apple-growers, lobster men and fishermen of Nova Scotia and the maritime provinces generally. Will the minister inform the committee what representations he has made to the provincial governments looking towards a reduction in the provincial gasoline taxes to relieve those classes of people who, I think it will be recognized, are least able to pay excessive taxation and who are profiting the least from expenditures arising out of the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No representations have
been made. It is not regarded by the federal government as its function to equalize all taxes in all the provinces. Some provinces rely upon some types of taxation, and other provinces rely upon other types. The dominion

Special War Revenue Act

government does not consider that it is its concern to equalize, for example, the profits on liquor sold in the various provinces. It might be the policy of one province to price its liquor in such a way as to secure a high profit per unit, and the policy of another province to get a low profit per unit. Similarly with gasoline, some provinces may as a matter of policy wish to rely largely upon the gasoline tax for their revenue, and other provinces not to so great an extent. If we were in the business of equalizing the varying taxes of the provinces, I do not know just what standard we should adopt. If we took the lowest tax in Canada as the standard, it would mean a great sacrifice of revenue to the province with the highest tax. If we took an intermediate tax, we would be busying ourselves to get the imposition of higher taxes in those provinces with a lower tax. There are some fields of taxation, namely, provincial fields, in which we would probably lie told that we should mind our own business if we started to say that this or that tax should go off or go on, and probably those who told us that would be right. We consider for the reasons we have given that for the duration of the war we should be permitted exclusive occupation of the income and corporation tax fields, and it is for that reason we have made our offer to the provinces, but it does not extend to all taxes.

In Nova
Scotia the income-tax payer is brought up to the highest tax level of any income-tax payer in Canada, although we have never had a provincial income tax in Nova Scotia. We are now being called upon to pay the highest gasoline tax in Canada. Nova Scotia and, indeed, the maritime provinces generally, as well as, I think, all the other provinces are receiving considerable revenues accruing from war activities, and I believe it would be a fair proposal for the minister to make to the maritime provinces, that they should reduce their gasoline tax-if the minister himself is not able to arrange this through the federal exchequer-to a level with that of the other provinces, thereby making a direct contribu-. tion to the war and relieving the user of gasoline in Nova Scotia-the farmer, the apple grower, the lobster fisherman and the ordinary motorist-from this increased and excessive gasoline tax. Not only is there a gasoline tax of thirteen cents a gallon in Nova Scotia, but there is also a sales tax of eight per cent. In this connection I would ask the minister whether the sales tax will apply on this excise tax which is being imposed. The sales tax ordinarily applies not only on the cost of the goods but also on the amount of duties paid on imported goods.

Well, all farmers are having their difficulties in these days. I rise only to answer
some of the statements made this afternoon which I believe, are a bit unfair. Some hon. members are trying to make it appear that everyone who has spoken this afternoon by way of protest is opposed to the imposition of this tax on gasoline.
