Someone spoke about the general application of this tax. He wanted everybody exempted. In most instances those who are using gasoline for business purposes have some means of passing on the extra cost of their operations to their customers. The government however, has set the price at which the fanner must sell his commodity; it has also put a restriction on the quantity which he is allowed to produce. The farmer is not even permitted storage on the grain which he himself grows over and above his quota.
A return was tabled here the other day which showed that a government-built elevator, which cost this country one and a half million dollars, was being leased to a firm for about $70,000 a year. The capacity of that elevator is three and a quarter million bushels, which, at eight cents a bushel, would bring in about $260,000 a year. What I am trying to point out is that the farmer is unable to bear this tax because he is cribbed and confined as regards what he can obtain from the growing of grain, let alone storing it.
The agricultural policy of the government in the last few years has compelled the western farmer to take up larger and larger farming units. The Minister of Agriculture will admit that the cheapest way of growing grain in western Canada is by mechanized farming- tractor farming. This is going to penalize the only farmers who can grow grain economically. I am one of those who regret very much that tractor farming has been forced upon the people of the west. I am one of those who believe that the half-section farm, the home farm, with more horses and cattle and mixed farming in most areas, would be better. But the economic policies of the government have ruined such farms. The Minister of Agriculture knows that drought and horse disease in the west have compelled many farmers to get rid of their horses and their stock and to take up tractor farming.
I do not know where the Minister of Agriculture got his figures with regard to tractors used in Canada, but I suggest that they are very much out of date. I believe the figures given by the bureau of statistics show that in 1936 there were over 81,000 tractors in the west alone, in the three prairie provinces.

What year?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It is dated May 5, 1941, about as late as one could get it.

I understand there were
105.000	in Canada ten years ago. We shall probably settle this a little later, but I know that a large number of tractors have been sold in the west this spring, because the farmers are realizing that they cannot get labour at the price they can afford.

Did the hon. member say
105.000	in all Canada or in the west alone?
In 1931, according to the census, there were 107,000.
In all Canada?

Yes. I do not think anyone questions the government's need of money to-day; we must have money. The minister will not encounter any argument on that. The only question, so far as Canada is concerned, is as to who can best pay, and we maintain that the farmer who uses gasoline will be affected indirectly in his threshing bill and is, therefore, one of those least able to pay the tax. Who can best pay? An hon. member yesterday said that the west has received a lot of subsidies and now is not satisfied and will not pay this tax. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, speaking last year about the reduction in the price of wheat from ninety cents to seventy cents, said, "We are asking the farmers to make this contribution of twenty cents a bushel as their part in the great war effort." A few months later the Minister of Agriculture put out a pamphlet telling the farmers not to grow wheat, to reduce their income by almost $100,000,000, in order to help Canada win the war. Now the Minister of Finance asks the farmers to make a further contribution. The farmer naturally wonders whether he is bearing more than his reasonable share of the burden, and that is the important consideration. When he takes up the Montreal Gazette, he reads about such matters as the improved showing by Dominion Woollens, their operating profit having more than doubled and their position being strengthened. Their net profit in 1939 was $113,934 and, in 1940, $229,779.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Before or after taxation?

After. On common
shares in 1939 the dividend was twenty-five cents and, in 1940, $1.03. The farmer remembers that industry went on strike in 1939. At that time the government undertook to limit profits on war contracts to five per cent.

Special War Revenue Act
Industry went on strike in 1939 when we vitally needed war equipment. The cabinet set aside the profit limitations bill, and industry is making profits to-day. But it is realized that the farmer is not receiving even the cost of production. This taxation and the regulations placed upon him are taking away every bit of equity he has in his home. When the equity is taken out of the homes and factories of every one. in Canada, then the farmer will figure that he is being treated equally with others. Hundreds of men in the west have enlisted because it is the only way of providing for their wives and families. But the excess profits tax just cuts into seventy-five per cent of what the industrialist makes over and above his average in the past few years. Does anyone expect the Canadian people to support an administration which is so inequitable in its distribution of taxes? I repeat, the policies of the government and the regulations imposed upon agriculture are wiping out the last bit of equity which many farmers have in their homes, and I know what I am talking about. The burden on agriculture is ruining that industry. _
The Minister of Finance was quite considerate of others when discussing the income tax. He said that if you went on taxing these people of high income, it would mean the liquidation of a large number of their homes. There are not more than 290,000 people in Canada, about thirteen per cent of the population, who are paying income tax, but there are millions of farm homes that are being ruined. There is liquidation of farm homes on a large scale. The farmers of the west are not begging. Someone suggested yesterday that we were always presenting the case of the farmers as if they were mendicants. The farmers are merely asking through their representatives for that small share of justice which is their birthright. They will learn from the events in this house how many of those who, they believe, are their friends are really betraying them.
I oppose this tax as being levied upon those least able to pay, those who are going to suffer more than any other group in Canada under the present policies of this administration-the farmers of the dominion.

The hon. gentleman being so
anxious to do something for farmers, why not let us argue this question from the point of view of extremes? If we do so, we shall get a point of view that will show up the ridiculousness of the argument. I am a farmer. Why should I not ask for exemption from the gasoline tax or the added tax that I have to pay on my automobile when I buy one?
Is that part of your production cost?

The automobile is just about as necessary to-day as the tractor; it serves a valuable purpose so far as marketing the farmers' products is concerned, just about as valuable as the tractor's contribution to production.

Why not use the
horse and buggy?
I do not wish to take time splitting hairs.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I would remind hon. members that they should not interrupt the speaker who has the floor, except with leave in order to ask a question.

I do not like to argue if it is possible to avoid it; I would rather trust the people, let them use their common sense. Remember that this law which protects us in the enjoyment of our rights in Canada, including our rights as members of parliament to speak, is the same law that is seeking to get the wherewithal to protect society in the enjoyment of these great possessions against the most violent and vicious enemy that ever befouled this earth. To argue for days and days over the little bit of money that we as farmers will pay in gasoline tax is, it seems to me, straining at a gnat and swallowing a camel. If we as farmers think we should be exempt from responsibility to contribute something to this war effort, why is a claim not made to be exempted for postage; let the farmer frank his letters on the rural mail.

Some farmers here
do that.

If an hon. member has any weakness himself he generally blames other people for the very thing of which he is guilty. If we follow the argument of the hon. member for Weyburn we might increase the . postage rate to five cents to the general public and exempt the farmers.
Postage does not enter into the cost of production.
Give him a free suit too.
Or we might ask exemption from the tax on sugar.

Sugar does
not enter into the cost of production.
Or exempt him from the tax on beer. We might exempt the farmer from all these taxes.

He does not want that, he is ready to pay his share.
Special War Revenue Act
It seems to me, as I listened to these arguments, that sometimes it is only by bringing up an extreme ease one can expose the foolishness of the arguments.

There has been a long discussion of this item; a good many hon. members are of opinion that it has been too long; but no discussion that has taken place since I have come to parliament has restored, or tended to restore my confidence in parliament as this discussion has. This is simply a protest against a generally destructive tax structure which is being forced on Canada at the present time. The hon. members who have protested so strongly on this three-cent tax on gasoline have, I believe, merely chosen this as a trench at which to give battle. The whole debate has been of a high order; there has not been overmuch foolish talk, not much pure retort just for its own sake. A short time ago an hon. member said a great deal of noise was being made. How else can hon. members register their protests except by making a noise? It is like what we see going on in the newspapers to-day; some newspapers seem to think that because members of parliament who come to parliament, a place to talk, do talk, they are not doing the country's work. Those papers need to readjust their thinking. Also there was some accusation of axe-grinding. That, I think, is utterly unjustified.
One statement in the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture I was glad to hear, namely, that this is a revenue-producing tax. Since the war broke out, there has been a great deal of what might be called "pussyfooting", an attempt being made on the part of the people in power to show that they are taxing to limit consumption and thereby prevent inflation. The Minister of Agriculture has frankly said that the object of this tax is to gain revenue. Once that is granted, we are on a basis from which we can proceed.
I shall say very little about that now; we may talk about it later.
It has been pointed out that only a few farmers have tractors. Those are grain farmers generally. Grain farmers are the ones who are literally being crucified to-day. The very men that the government and everyone else were kow-towing to in the last war are to-day for the very same kind of national service *being crucified. Practically all the grain farmers, at least those in the west who work on a large scale, are getting tractors; they are forced to or else they cannot compete successfully with those who have tractors.
Something was said about non-farmers speaking for farmers. That is absolute nonsense. If anyone takes the stand that no hon. member can speak for a class unless he fMr. Quelch.]
is a member of that class, then it would be utterly impossible for the people of this country to be represented in this house. Surely there are bound to be lawyers representing miners and doctors representing loggers. Let us have an end to this nonsense of sneering at men who speak for farmers when they do not happen at the moment to be farmers themselves.
The question has been raised whether the tax is on all the farmers in Canada. Does any other class of producer in this country stand to suffer as much as the farmers will as a result of the imposition of this tax? We have not the figures to determine accurately the answer to that question, but certainly it is a thought-provoking question.
The Minister of Agriculture gave what I considered a reasonable speech, effective, as his speeches usually are. He spoke of 107,000 tractors in Canada, and the impression I got was that he was endeavouring to convey to the committee that the measure of the farmers' participation in the payment of this tax was the number of tractors they had. Let us remember that more and more the farmers of this country are getting cars. They must have cars, and all the farmers who have cars will pay this tax. In addition to the cost of production through the tractor, the amount a farmer has to pay to go to town to see his banker will certainly be represented in his cost of production.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

When the committee took recess, Mr. Chairman, I was commenting upon the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture, in the course of which he had pointed out that there were only 107,000 tractors in Canada, apparently thereby intending to imply that the cost to the farming population by reason of the three-cent tax on gasoline was not such a serious matter as a number of the opponents of that tax appeared to consider it. I pointed out that apparently the minister had overlooked the fact that every farmer who owns a car which he uses in his business also pays, on the gasoline which he uses in that car, a tax which enters into his cost of production as well as into the cost of living. I was about to point out that not only do farmers keep cars nowadays but that practically every farmer, of any importance, in the west at least, must have a truck. Generally that truck uses gasoline, and on the gasoline

Special War Revenue Act
the farmer buys for that truck he must also pay a tax which enters into his cost of production. I was going to remind the minister that many of our farmers use gasoline engines for other kinds of farm work, such as running choppers and so forth, and that on the gasoline used for those sources of power they will also pay a tax which also will add to the cost of production.
I should now like to turn to the question in a general way. I think what is principally wrong with the minister and his advisers, in connection with this gasoline tax and a good many other taxes that are being imposed in this budget, is that they have failed to distinguish between gasoline as a luxury and gasoline as a necessity. I do not think any of those who have opposed this measure have argued that a tax should not be collected on gasoline used as a luxury. Some have even advocated a higher tax, up to six cents a gallon. I am not in a position to offer any suggestion in that respect, but I think it is fair that gasoline used as a luxury should pay a tax. On the other hand, gasoline that is used as a necessity is in an altogether different class. So far as the farmers in my area are concerned-and I can speak for no other area-the result of the imposition of this gasoline tax, and a great many of the other taxes imposed this year, will be demoralizing; they will bring about a deterioration and disintegration on the part of those people. I think one hon. member who spoke just before I rose pointed out that a great many farmers, driven to desperation by the conditions under which they have been forced to struggle, are giving it all up and enlisting in order to make a living.
I would point out to the committee that a farmer is one of the most precious possessions a state can have. Once that farmer is destroyed, he cannot be readily replaced. While I am on this point, may I add that apparently there is altogether too great a tendency on the part of some people to take a short-range view of this war and to assume that probably it will be over in a year. If we assume that, Mr. Chairman, we are taking a serious responsibility upon ourselves. This war may go on for ten years. I shall talk about this at greater length later on, but we must be prepared for a time when perhaps, in order to get a pound of butter to Britain, we shall have to send three pounds from Canada. Still it will be our duty to supply that butter; if we now destroy the men who are in a position to produce the butter, the bacon, the wheat and all the other farm products that may be required, the day will come when we shall
repent in more than sackcloth and ashes. The men who are designing the tax structure which is producing this deterioration will stand condemned before this and all future generations. We must distinguish between the gasoline that is used as a luxury and the gasoline that is a necessity.
The next misapprehension under which the minister is labouring-I would go so far as to call it an absolute delusion-is that all the money this government obtains must come from taxation and borrowing. I make no further comment than that; but I do say that if the minister sternly-I would almost say stubbornly-adheres to the idea that all *the money he needs to run this war must come from taxing or borrowing from the people of Canada, then he is making one of the greatest errors ever made by a man occupying his position in this country.
I wish now to point out that the minister is forcing on inflation. The other day I received in the mail a fine article, apparently inspired by someone interested in the welfare of the Liberal party in Canada, pointing out how we were financing this war without inflation, and so on, and so on. I would point out to the minister that the steps he is taking now are forcing on inflation in spite of everything that can be done to prevent it; for by the taxes he is imposing in this budget he is forcing up the prices of practically all kinds of commodities as they come into the hands of the consumer from one end to the other of this country; and that, sir, is inflation, a rise in prices. Once or twice already I have pointed out, and I am going to point out again with all the sincerity and earnestness of which I am capable, that inflation or a rise in prices can also result from a scarcity of goods. If, as a result of these iniquitous measures which are being taken to-day, the ability of Canada to produce goods is impaired, then by the same measures the danger of future inflation in Canada is being enhanced. This tax on gasoline will tend to increase the prices of commodities and destroy the productive power of Canada. Possibly, as the hon. member for Temiscouata said the other night, the men who are devising the tax structure of Canada are a group of experimenters. Probably to some extent they have to be; but they need not be reckless; they need not be stubborn, and they need not be callous.
I now come to deal in some detail with the effect of this gasoline tax on the farmer, and it is of the farmer I speak because my constituency is, in the main, a farming district. I have said something already about the increased cost of transporting farm goods. Let it be understood by 'hon. members of this
Special War Revenue Act

committee, Mr. Chairman, that in my riding there are many farmers who cannot take their children to school without using a car; and the gasoline tax will have the effect of increasing the cost of giving those children an education. Let it be borne in mind that many of them have no other means of going to church or to any other social gathering. The days of the horse and buggy have passed; we must recognize that fact. There may be other parts of Canada in which that is not the situation, but it is the situation in the west. In my travels I have seen a few horses and buggies in Ontario and Quebec, but I have not seen one for years in my constituency. The car has taken their place. An increase in the cost of gasoline means an increased cost of living for the farmers so far as transportation is concerned. As I pointed out this afternoon, if the farmer comes to town to buy some goods, to see his banker or to attend upon any other matter of business, he must pay this tax. Thereby he has increased, not only his cost of production but his cost of living. That is a serious matter.
I have referred already to the use of trucks. Many of the farmers in my riding simply could not market their products without trucks. Some of them have not a wagon, and many of them have not teams capable of going on the road. The result is that, no matter how much they might desire to do what the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Wood) advocates they should do, they cannot. We must make allowance for this fact in a country like Canada. In many instances our farmers live altogether too far from their markets, altogether too far from their social centres to use teams and wagons, even if they had them. Horses are not to be found, and if they could be found the necessary pasturage would be lacking. That is how conditions have changed in wide areas of Alberta and Saskatchewan.
I have also commented upon the use of gasoline in washing, running pumps, grinders, and all that sort of thing, a daily necessity to many farmers. The hon. member for Brant hinted that if farmers could afford to buy all these appurtenances or aids to easier living, then they should be in position to pay a higher tax. But these farmers have simply moved into a condition of life where pumps, grinders and so forth are necessary. If they do not have them, their economy is thrown off balance and they are not able to make it go.
There is another aspect to this tax which is of considerable concern and which has not been stressed before the committee. I refer to the effect of this increase upon the truck 
and bus companies. One of the most serious disabilities from which a number of provinces are suffering is high railroad rates, and one source of relief from this condition in Saskatchewan and Alberta, and I believe also in Manitoba, is the truck and bus companies. A further tax upon gasoline will unquestionably bring about higher rates and thereby injure those people who have had to depend upon such companies for transportation. This will also increase the cost of living. It has been argued by some that we must conserve gasoline. I was going to say something about that, but the Minister of Agriculture has said that this tax is being imposed in order to raise revenue. Therefore I shall not say much about consumption.
In passing, however, I would ask: If we are concerned about conserving gasoline, why should we not go to work to produce alcohol in this country? Some people will say that that cannot be done economically. The day must come in Canada when we all will realize that what is physically possible is financially possible. If we can produce potatoes in great abundance and make alcohol therefrom, then our Canadian economy can afford to do it. If we cannot afford to do it, then it devolves upon the people in charge of this country to see that such conditions are brought about as will enable us to do it. How can we in Canada say that we cannot afford to produce motor fuel from potatoes when certain countries which we all have in mind can do so?
I understand that alcohol can be made from wheat. The process is a little expensive, but it can be done. If we are really concerned about saving gasoline, if we are afraid that we may run into a shortage, then it is high time that we began to plan to produce fuel from one or another of the products of which we have an abundance or of which we can produce an abundance.
I think I have had my say in this matter. With many of the statements that have been made, I heartily agree. I do not wish to be critical, but I urge the minister to get away from the idea that all the money required to run a first-class war in this stream-lined age can be raised by borrowing or taxation.
If the minister persists in following that line of thought, he will be treating this magnificent country as an inexpert driver might an automobile or any other high-class machine. He will mismanage it until it finishes up a hopeless and chaotic wreck on the side of the road.
I am sure the minister does not want that to occur, but it is quite possible to bring this country to the condition I have indicated.
I urge the minister to reconsider this gaso-

line tax and several of the other taxes, about which I shall have something to say as we go along.
Am I right in understanding that this tax will not apply on distillate or diesel fuel?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: How about diesel fuel?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It does not include diesel fuel.

It will not apply to
kerosene?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
Should a mixture of so-called white gasoline and distillate be produced, I suppose the definition given by the minister would determine whether or not it would be subject to the tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

In this particular crisis when economy is the slogan of the times, I have refrained from taking up any of the time of this committee by participating in this debate. I have listened to the speeches that have been made since this resolution came before the committee, some of them eloquent, some of them bordering on the heroic and some of them possessing other attributes which I need not mention at the present time. I am rising to-night, first, to relieve myself of the trying ordeal of attempting to be an appreciative audience to all these speeches and, second, to give the reasons to the committee and to my constituency why I have not risen in protest against this impost on gasoline.
Ninety-five per cent of my constituents are farmers and fishermen. These people are suffering all the burdens and trials being borne by the farmers of the west or central Canada, but I have not received one protest from them against the imposition of this tax. The members of this house may think I have been delinquent in carrying out the desires of my constituency; but I take second place to no one, Mr. Chairman, in representing as well as I possibly can my constituents, and if I had 14873-194
Special War Revenue Act
received even a fraction of a protest from my constituency against this tax I would have risen in my place before to-night. Not a single protest, however, have I received from farmers or fishermen in my constituency. Therefore I am not going to pose before the parliamentary footlights as a champion defending the people against an impost which they in fact welcome and approve. They are absolutely willing to assume and desirous of assuming this tax as a little part of the war effort in order to carry us through to a successful victory in this war against insecurity.

Having listened to the speeches delivered in this committee in the last few days, I regret exceedingly that the Minister of Finance will not take my advice. He erred once in not taking my advice when he passed certain items.
Does the minister see what I have in my hand and what I am going to speak of? I think I am perfectly in order in congratulating a member of this house who has been honoured in a signal way. Although I am not familiar with Beauchesne, I think it is quite in order to congratulate or console a member of this house upon an added honour or burden that may have been placed upon him. The other day a friend of mine went to the town of Waterloo, and in order to assist the Minister of Finance in this troublesome period he conceived the idea of selling old-fashioned mottoes such as, "If it does not rain to-day, it will be fine to-morrow." He also sold a motto of universal support and popularity! -"Forgive us; we did not know what we were doing." One of the most popular members of this house has been accorded a great honour to-day, I can speak, if not on behalf of the party opposite, certainly on behalf of the rump, when I extend to the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), our hearty congratulations and our sincerest sympathy with him with regard to the extreme honour which has been conferred upon him to-day. I saw in the Ottawa Journal to-day that the most popular member of the party to my left and one of the most esteemed gentlemen in the house has been appointed Conservative organizer for the dominion. I also saw in the Ottawa Journal a reference to "23" being that hon. gentleman's lucky number. It reminded me of the days of my youth when I used to see in the paper a little cap advertised as "23 skidoo." I salute, congratulate and sympathize with the hon. member for Peel; sympathy he will need.

To my mind, the increase the minister has mentioned in the tax on wine up to forty cents a gallon is entirely inadequate in comparison with the tax which has been placed on gasoline. I had on the order paper some time ago a question *which stated that a delegation, representing the Roman Catholic church, the Church of England, the United church, the Baptist church and a number of other churches waited on the government-
Not all of them.

-with a view of
having the consumption of beer, wine and spirituous liquors decreased; and I was not well satisfied with the information given. Is the minister in a position to inform us as to the attitude of the government to that delegation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

No. I was not one of the
members of the cabinet who received that delegation, and I do not know what representations they made. I have not a clear recollection of the circumstances.

To my mind, this is
a luxury commodity, and a tax of forty cents a gallon is entirely too low. In past years we have
invariably had strong representations from the farmers, growers of grapes, who protested against the increase of these taxes. This year they have not made those representations. 9.	That there shall be imposed, levied and collected an excise tax of twenty per cent on the admission price to a moving picture theatre, payable by the moving picture exhibitor.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On this resolution I wish
to make a statement to the committee, and to have the following amendment moved:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the resolution proposing amendments to the Special War Revenue Act. introduced on April twenty-ninth, one thousand nine hundred and forty-one, by adding to resolution 9 thereof the following words:-
"and a like tax of twenty per cent on certain other forms of amusement, the said tax to come into effect on a date to be proclaimed by the governor in council."

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I so move.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The committee will, of course, ask at once what other forms of amusement it is proposed to tax. Let me say at this point that all this will be set out fully in the bill, but I will tell the committee what I intend to have written into the bill.
My proposals are: to impose a tax on amusements for which an admission fee is charged and in which those admitted do not themselves participate. This is not to cover persons who pay to go into a place to bowl, or something of that sort; it relates to the type of amusement where those admitted are admitted as spectators. The twenty per cent tax, if this proposal is accepted, will apply to all of those amusements, with power, however, to the Minister of National Revenue in his discretion to exempt from the tax amusements which are not held regularly or in accordance with a prearranged schedule, or where there is no gain or profit to those promoting, organizing, conducting or sponsoring them, or where the entire proceeds are devoted to charitable, religious or patriotic purposes. I believe that sums up almost completely the proposals which the government is placing before the committee regarding the extension of this tax to other amusements.
Does that mean the net proceeds?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The language will be much more specific than that. All I ask the committee to do at the moment is to pass this 14873-194}
amendment to the resolution which is in the terms I have read. Members of the committee realize, I assume, that a resolution does not need to be too specific-I am told that resolutions down through the years have become increasingly specific-when the resolution is for the purpose of giving notice of legislation, and so long as it is in terms wide and general enough to cover the legislation. The specific details may be contained in the legislation rather than in the resolution.
With regard to this matter of the amusement tax, it was found that attendance at motion-picture theatres, which are the most general form of amusement and which cover the nation, is increasing rapidly. I cannot give the specific figures to the committee. It was found also that extensive plans were being made for the building of large numbers of new motion-picture theatres, and it was also found that there was an increasing demand on the part of the public that the federal government, in this time of war and great need, should obtain some revenue from the vast sums of money which are being spent by the people of Canada on this general form of entertainment. Therefore this tax, which is the heavy tax of twenty per cent, was suggested in the budget.
The majority of admissions to motion-picture theatres in Canada are at the rate of twenty-five cents, and this tax means that thirty cents will be substituted for the present twenty-five cent admission charge. It was regarded by the motion-picture industry as very heavy, but my belief is that to charge the public thirty cents, instead of twenty-five cents, for going to picture shows is not, under present conditions, unreasonable or excessive. Moreover, I very much doubt whether it will greatly curtail the attendance. Our experience of recent months in the imposition of taxes has been astonishing. Last December we imposed taxes on automobiles and on a wide variety of consumer durable goods, expecting that the consumption of these- goods would thereby be materially curtailed, but it did not seem to have that effect. Retail sales all over the country are up substantially, and I am inclined to think that, even with this additional five cents on the twenty-five cent ticket, there will not be a substantial reduction in attendances at the motion-picture theatres.
What will be the addition to a thirty-five cent ticket?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Seven cents. It would be forty-two cents. The motion-picture people said at once that we should not single them out. They said that this was the poor man's amusement and that we were taxing the poor man and not the rich man.

Special War Revenue Act
They were right in that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think it is fair to describe the motion picture as the poor man's amusement. I believe all classes of society go to see moving pictures. Some people take the loges; some, the orchestra; some, the balcony, but all go to see the moving pictures, and I am unable to accept the argument that it is the poor man's form of amusement. The motion-picture people, however, did so describe it, and they made a strong plea to have the tax extended to other forms of amusement.
To make a general rigid application of this twenty per cent tax to all other forms of amusement would create tremendous difficulties. The kinds of amusement that are ordinarily cited as being those that should be taxed are the theatres, which are to some extent in competition with the motion-picture shows and where the tickets cost much more than the motion-picture tickets. There was not much difficulty about the theatres except that there are theatrical performances which are put on by dramatic leagues, by girls in ladies colleges and by little amateur groups of one sort or another who get out of the admission fee only enough and sometimes not enough to pay expenses.
We realized when we were dealing with that type of theatrical production that we would be dealing with something entirely different from the motion-picture industry, where the tax is collected from well-established and, in many instances, corporate entities, who keep books that can be audited, where little difficulty about the collection of the tax is anticipated, and who are on a strictly profit-making basis. It was realized that if the tax were to be extended to theatres, there would have to be some power of exemption, and I think the classes of exemptions which could be granted, but which need not be granted if the minister in his discretion thinks they should not be granted, are of a kind regarding which the minister should have the power to grant exemption. They are pretty well summed up under the three headings I have already given, namely, where performances are not held regularly or in accordance with a prearranged schedule, where there is no gain or profit to those promoting, organizing, conducting or sponsoring them, or where the entire profits are devoted to charitable, religious or patriotic purposes. I do not say that in the administration of the legislation the minister will grant exemption in all these cases, but I think he should have the power to grant 
exemptions in the cases indicated; otherwise there will be hardship particularly with regard to small, sporadic, non-profit making amateur theatrical productions. I am quite sure there would be. We had, therefore, to take that power of exemption.
The same considerations apply to athletic contests. I do not think that in all instances admission should be taxed. Hon. members will have in their own minds country baseball leagues where teams from two towns put on a game. They charge an admission fee; it may be ten or fifteen or twenty-five cents for a man and his wife, and the proceeds of the game are no more than sufficient to pay expenses. There may be something over out of which baseball bats, mitts, uniforms and so forth will have to be bought; but for the federal government to step in, in all these cases which do not come within the class of amusements which the public desire to have taxed, or which would not yield much revenue, or the taxing of which could not be satisfactorily administered, would, in my opinion, be a mistake. There is, therefore, power in the minister to grant exemption there, and under the same headings and for the same reasons I mentioned with regard to theatres. We could go down the line.
Mr. MacNICOL; Weekly bingo games.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the bingo games the
spectators participate. I know that we are walking right into a field in which the discussion is going to be quite interesting and extensive and one man's opinion will be equal in value to any other's, with the result that the debate may go on for days. I would, however, ask hon. members not to try to get one hundred per cent complete equity in this matter because it can never be attained. It may be that there are some bingo games to which admission is charged where it would be more proper from every point of view for us to take twenty per cent of the proceeds than it would be from some hockey game. I do not know. I am sure, however, that it would not do for us to take general power to reach out and take money everywhere that people are amusing themselves. I do not think that would do at all. We had better stick to the line between the kind of performances in which those paying admission are spectators and those performances in which the people paying admission participate. I am willing to answer questions.

Why does the minister think it is fair to take the gasoline tax from everyone and not the amusement tax? What

Special War Revenue Act
about taking a tax from the man who pays two or three dollars for a ticket to a hockey match?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He will be taxed.

Where do local fairs,
school fairs, exhibitions, church socials and other such amusements come in?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot be too specific, but there is power of exemption there for one or another of the three reasons given. Probably the fairs which the hon. gentleman has in mind would come under one of those heads.

Would they have to
make application?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To the Minister of National Revenue.

Are we to understand
from this wording that the date at which the tax will come into operation applies only to the tax referred to in the amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Can the minister give
any undertaking or state his opinion as to how long delayed that date may be? The motion-picture people may suffer inequality for a considerable time if some statement is not made as to the date.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It may be a few weeks- as soon as it can be organized. I do not admit that the motion-picture people are suffering by reason of the fact that others are not taxed. It is not a question of their suffering but of their feeling that if they are paying other people should pay. It is not a matter of their losing business as a result of others not being taxed. I am satisfied of that.

First I must congratulate the minister upon giving some consideration and taking some of the discrimination out of this item. Let me say that theatre owners in Canada do not object to paying a tax, but they do object to paying a tax that is an impossible tax. In his budget speech the minister indicated that he was trying to stop public spending in order that the people in the lower income brackets may have more money to invest in war savings stamps and certificates; yet in the very next breath he takes seven or eight millions out of their pockets by placing a twenty per cent tax on the gross income of theatres. The minister has already stated that he does not agree that the moving-picture theatre is the low-salaried man's recreation. I can say to him from twenty-five years' experience that the motion picture is the labouring man's recreation; there is no
doubt whatever about that. If the moving-picture theatre operators had to depend upon people in the higher income brackets, they certainly would not be in business very long.
I understand that representations were made to the minister immediately after his budget speech. I feel certain that it was the minister's intention, when he brought in this budget, that this twenty per cent tax should be paid by the motion-picture exhibitors and not passed on the patrons of the theatre.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; that was never my intention.

Well, I accept that, but I wonder whether the minister did not spend many weary hours considering this particular tax. If hon. members look through the whole of the resolutions, they will not find one other line of business that is taxed to anywhere near the extent of twenty per cent of the gross receipts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What about cigarette paper tubes?
Mr. TUSTIN. That is one exception.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And wines?

On wine it is only forty cents a gallon, which is, I think, nowhere near twenty per cent of the cost of the wine.
I have already taken this matter up with the minister privately; I have made a suggestion to him in writing; I have urged upon him that a sliding scale be applied to theatres. I agree that possibly in some of the large centres where there are large war industries and where great numbers of soldiers are stationed there may be a great increase in theatre attendance. In the small centres, however, the towns and villages where there are no war works and no soldiers stationed, the attendance has not increased; and with this increase of seven cents on the normal thirty-five cent ticket, which is the prevailing price in the small centres, the attendance will suffer. Of that there is no doubt.
I have in my hand a telegram I received to-day from a person who put this tax into effect about two weeks ago, thinking it was compulsory to put it into effect when first announced; he advises me that in the few days that it was in effect the attendance decreased over twenty-five per cent.
I urge the minister to give consideration to the small centres, because in a great many instances the motion-picture theatre is the only recreation that some people have. The minister says that my suggestion may be hard to control or operate. The tax could be easily operated on a sliding scale. In towns of
Special War Revenue Act

5,000 population, 10,000 population, he would have no difficulty whatsoever. Now that he has added these other amusements to the tax list, there is no doubt that his revenue would be even more than it would be if he left the twenty per cent on all the motion-picture theatres.
One other matter I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. In Ontario during the last period when we had a tax on motion-picture theatre tickets, men in uniform in all branches of the service were exempted. I would suggest that since this is a dominion measure, the minister should see to it that the men of our fighting forces, the army, navy and air force, are exempt from this tax.
I do not wish to take further time, but I again urge upon the minister that he give consideration to placing this tax on a sliding scale whereby there will be some relief for theatres in the smaller centres.

We are perhaps spending, on these resolutions, a good deal of time that might be saved by deferring discussion until the bill is introduced. The very fact that, when a resolution as important as this comes before the committee, the minister, as a result of representations made to him, and of the attitude hon. members took on the budget speech, finds that he needs must move an amendment to it, shows only too plainly to me that perhaps too many of our budget resolutions are devised in a panicky way. Had the minister had some practical-I say that quite sincerely-representations made to him; had some men with practical knowledge of the situation in Canada been sitting in with him, instead of some of the brain-trust that we have had running this country for some time, many of these resolutions might have been more or less modified before they were brought into the house.

There would be no taxes
at all if one listened to the fellows who are interested.

If one listened to the
brain-trust there would be nothing but taxes. The whole situation is that the minister provided for certain forms of taxation. Two days were wasted in discussion of the gasoline tax-
Three days.

Not entirely wasted, because hon. members put their views before the committee, feeling that certain modifications of that tax could be made. As a result of the government's desire to raise revenue they have said, "We must levy a tax of 
twenty per cent on the gross proceeds of theatres." The day the budget came down, that became an immediately effective tax on the theatres of this country. Then, two or three days after, certain protests were made not only by hon. members speaking here on the budget debate, but by theatre owners and those interested in theatres throughout, the dominion. Therefore one day the minister rose in his place and said, "We have to change the date when this tax shall come into force to May 19.'' That enabled these theatre owners, who will not have to pay the tax, to be in a position to pass it on to the public. This shows conclusively that there was not given to the levying of this tax the thought that should have been given. When a province levies an amusement tax, it says to those operating the places of amusement, "You purchase from the government a roll of tickets, for which you pay according to the admission you intend to charge." In that way the government immediately receives the tax represented by that number of tickets. If any tickets are left in the roll, they are returned to the government and a refund is made. In some instances, where a concert or other entertainment is put on and the tickets cannot be obtained at once from the government, the people go to the local theatre and purchase tax tickets there. There has been no difficulty at all in collecting the amusement tax in Ontario.
The federal government has said, "There are many millions of dollars spent in motion-picture theatres in this country each year. This is a waste of money and we must have part of it. We are going to see to it that some of that money comes to us." The minister says that this is not a poor man's amusement. He must know that if in any community, be it a village, town or city, you could rule out the working class or low income group, there would not be enough people left to patronize three theatres in the whole of Ontario. The people who enjoy motion pictures are the people who stand at machines from morning until night or from night until morning, and then go to a matinee in the afternoon. This is a poor man's amusement. Of all those who attend motion-picture theatres in this country, seventy-seven per cent go to theatres where the admission is twenty-five cents or less.
Just to show the inconsistency of the government in connection with this tax, during the budget debate I, together with other hon. members, said, "If you are going to tax the people who go to motion-picture theatres, so should you also tax those who can pay $5

Special War Revenue Act
for a ticket to a symphony concert, or those who can pay $2.50 for a ticket to hear Lily Pons," as some of us were privileged to do; "so should you tax those who go to the racetrack and pay $1.50, $2 or $2.50 admission; so should you tax the people who go to hockey games night after night and pay anywhere from seventy-five cents to $2.50 for a seat."
They are going to be taxed.

They were not going to be taxed until the amendment was brought down. It is only now that you people who are supporting the government are showing some sense and doing what is right. The man who goes to the grill room of the Chateau Laurier, or any other hotel in this country, and is able to pay a service charge of $1.50 should also pay a tax. These taxes are the easiest thing in the world to collect; at least the government of Ontario had no difficulty in collecting them. This afternoon and yesterday, however, amendment after amendment was ruled out of order because in those amendments hon. members sought to change another tax, and there was no assurance that the changes suggested would bring in the amount it was hoped to realize under the original proposal. But following protests from those operating motion-picture theatres, from members of this house and from others, the government now has signified its intention of extending this tax.
What is wrong with that?

The government have said, "We budgeted for so much money; this is the amount we require to carry on the activities of this country, in both peace time and war time, during the coming year." They estimated that the revenue from this tax would be so much; but because of the pressure that has been brought to bear, the government is now going to extend the application of that tax, which means that it will have a large sum of money it does not require, if the budget figures are to be believed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Don't worry.

Just wait a moment. The minister has budgeted for a certain amount of money from loans and a certain amount from taxation. If he wants to be fair with the people of this country; if he is going to extend this tax-which I think will meet with the approval of every member of this house- then at least he should reduce the tax on motion-picture theatre tickets, and other amusement tickets, to ten per cent. I have no doubt whatever that this could be done and
still bring in the amount of money originally estimated. If hon. members look at the record of the amount of money collected year after year by the Ontario government under its amusement tax, they will see that it amounted to about one-third of the amount you are expecting to collect under this tax. That is only one province; there are eight more provinces as well. The Minister of Finance laughs, as much as to say, "I expected this". All right. I have no interest in moving pictures, or in any other amusement than sitting in this House of Commons.
I wish to say in all sincerity, Mr. Chairman, that I do not know of anything that would be more beneficial in our war effort than to bring amusements of this kind, which are so necessary to the life of a people, especially in war time, within reach of the men and women- yes, and even the boys and girls who are leaving high school and going to work on the farms and in the factories of this country- who are engaged in war work. As I said in my speech on the budget, for a time in the United Kingdom they refused to permit the rebuilding of motion-picture theatres that had been bombed. Over there, a special permit has to be obtained, and cause shown, before any wrecked building can be rebuilt. It is, however, a fact that when a motion-picture theatre is bombed in the old country to-day, a permit is issued automatically for the rebuilding of that theatre, because they know how important it is that the people should have some surcease from the tremendous burdens of worry and work under which they labour from day to day. Therefore I say to the minister that if he has budgeted correctly-and I must take his word that he has-surely he could say to the Canadian people, "Instead of taxing these less expensive amusements so heavily, we will reduce the tax to ten per cent and spread it over a great many more people who otherwise would be exempt", so that they will pay what the poor man would have had to pay if the regulation had not been amended.

I have very little to say, much less than I would have said if the minister had not presented his amendments. I wish, however, to say a word for the motion-picture people. I believe there are twenty theatres in my riding, and I have seen these people donate the use of their theatres on many occasions in order to carry on recruiting meetings and so forth. This was particularly the situation in the last war, and I know, when the time comes in this war for such meetings, these people will give up their theatres freely. They are ready to do their part to carry on in the best interests of the country. Only
Special War Revenue Act

recently a number of theatres in my riding held meetings to assist in the work being carried on by the Minister of National War Services. They will do so again, and for that they deserve some consideration. I have no doubt that they will permit the use of their theatres in connection with the new war loan. We shall be seeing notices thrown on the screen asking us to buy the war loan, and most likely permission will be granted to people to go on the platforms to advocate the purchase of war loan bonds. That is all to the good; that is all in the interests of this dominion, and it is something for which the theatre owners should receive consideration. The hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox (Mr. Tustin) tells me that the theatres in his riding are now advertising the war salvage campaign. I notice that the minister nods his head, which shows that he appreciates the help being given.
As I say, the minister's amendment eliminates many of the complaints which I have received. I have here four or five telegrams, and I should like to read parts of these to the minister. The first is from the St. Clair theatre, and reads:
If my working class patrons can pay tax, why shouldn't patrons of higher priced amusements pay tax and share the burden?
I understand that these patrons of the higher priced amusements will now be taxed.
Not the same tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The twenty per cent tax.

That will eliminate the complaint voiced in this particular telegram. The people living in the immediate vicinity of this theatre are not wealthy; they are honest, thrifty working people.
Here is another wire from the College theatre, as follows:
As a member of the motion-picture industry I have always done everything to help the war effort and always will, but I protest against the unfair discrimination of the dominion excise tax on motion-picture theatres being exclusively directed against motion-picture patrons who are families of moderate means. Legitimate theatre, concert-goers, circus, carnival, dance-hall, baseball and hockey fans escape this tax. My patrons are poor people.
The minister's amendment eliminates most of the complaints voiced by this gentleman.
The next telegram is from the Belmont theatre at the comer of College and Dufferin streets, and reads:
The feeling is that the poor man is called upon to bear a burden not shared democratically by all classes, this mode of entertainment being singled out from all others for very high

taxation. Patriotism of the people unquestionable but demand democratic treatment. The people want and demand common justice to the working class families in the spirit of Canada's constitution.
I understand the minister's amendment provides for the taxation of all other amusements. Will it apply to baseball games?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Will race-meets like
those at the Woodbine and other tracks be taxed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Apparently the amendment takes care of this owner's complaints.
The next is from the Adelphi theatre, and reads:
If present conditions warrant taxes on amusements why not on sports, dances, race tracks, bingos, et cetera.
Will weekly dances held by fraternities or other institutions be subject to this tax of twenty per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; they escape.

Is that fair?
The next telegram is from the Lansdowne theatre, and reads:
The motion picture industry is one hundred per cent behind the government in its war effort. I am not objecting to the tax on theatres, in fairness to the industry and to the public the tax should be on a graded scale-
That is what was suggested by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox. I think some consideration should be given to what he has said. I have attended the show in Napanee, from which town the hon. member comes, and I would imagine that if they get one full show a night that would be the limit. The telegram continues:

and should not be such a burden to the small wage-earner who looks to the motion picture for his entertainment. The tax should apply to all forms of entertainment and not be confined to the motion-picture industry.
Am I correct in understanding that the tax is to apply on admissions of ten cents upward?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. Perhaps that answer
will give the wrong impression. There is really no lower limit; we do not start at ten cents even.

The vast majority of the 70,000 people whom I represent are honest, thrifty, working people. On Saturday afternoons I understand that most of the theatres allow the children in for ten cents. Their mothers send them to the theatres to get them off the streets. The programme on Saturday afternoons is usually made up of educational pictures, funnies, as well as

Special War Revenue Act
patriotic pictures. In my humble opinion there is nothing that will do more to increase the morale, certainly to retain the morale ol our people, than to have their children see patriotic pictures in which the British navy is fighting and British soldiers are winning. Would it be possible to differentiate between the tickets sold to children on Saturday afternoon and those sold to adults in the evening ?
I can see no reason why that could not be arranged because the tickets are sold at a lower rate to the children anyway. The amendment, while not relieving the moving-picture theatre owners from the tax, does relieve them from being the only ones on whom this tax is inflicted. Finally, I would ask the minister if it would not be possible to allow children's tickets on Saturday to be tax-free.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let me make the situation perfectly clear with regard to that. This tax is twenty per cent of the gross receipts, and it is payable by the motion-picture industry. It is payable by the owner or exhibitor.
It is up to him?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is up to him. If he wishes to allow anyone in at the old price, he may do so. He may load the tax in any proportions that suit him. He may charge more than twenty per cent increase on the higher priced tickets and nothing on the lower priced tickets. He may lower the price of the lower priced tickets. We are not doing what the provinces were doing, namely, imposing a direct tax on the patrons. The provinces had to impose a direct tax because they had no power to impose an indirect tax. We are imposing an indirect tax, a tax on the owners, proprietors or exhibitors of motion pictures-
But the minister will admit-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Just a minute.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
I should like to ask the minister a question. If the minister says no, all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The answer is, no. I am answering a question of the hon. member for Davenport.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister does not yield.
That is all right with me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is not very much reason why I should not have yielded except that I was in the middle of a sentence and was answering another hon. gentleman. I am
quite willing to answer the hon. member's question, but he must have a little respect for the rules of order.
I do not know just where I was in my statement.
The minister was explaining to the member for Davenport that the theatre owner could tax the children's tickets or the adult tickets as he saw fit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That Was it, and it was an indirect tax. I had not very much more to say.
As I understand it now. the theatre owner has to pay a twenty per cent tax on his gross receipts?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

That is a pretty stiff tax.
I do not know any other business or industry that is taxed twenty per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: What about the hon. member's own income?
I am speaking, not for myself but for the people of my riding, the working men.
Is the hon. member a working man?

Yes, I am, and there is no other man in the House of Commons who in his lifetime has worked harder than I have.
I like to go to picture shows. I think they are one of the greatest educational institutions in this country, and I hope this twenty per cent tax does not affect the great work of education that is being done by the picture shows. Twenty per cent, however, does seem to me a pretty heavy tax. I know the minister must have the money. I have made the protest which has been sent on to me, and since there is nothing more that I can do, I have done my duty.

It is quite apparent that, in the main at any rate, the minister appears to be receiving more commendation than criticism. I consider, however, that I should express one criticism with regard to the procedure this evening of introducing the amendment without any kind of notice whatever.
Didn't you caucus it this morning?

Could the minister not work out some form of compensation for a great deal of labour that has been lost? I would not say it is a case of love's labour lost, but at any rate it seems to me that there are indications in the committee this

Special War Revenue Act
evening that a considerable number of well-prepared speeches have been flattened out, and I think the minister might try to work out some way of compensating these poor people who have spent so much time in sharpening for his hide barbs which now they cannot use.

The hon. member who has just spoken has made a number of statements that certainly are not true. The members of the house are not here to get the minister's hide. From the very start of this budget the members of the opposition have been only too willing to help the minister get his budget resolutions through.
Oh!

Oh, yes, and a great deal of the criticism of the budget proposals came from members of the government's own party who had not the courage to vote for what they said in the house.
I rose a few minutes ago, when the minister was answering a question asked by the hon. member for Davenport, to put a question. Usually the minister is not discourteous in the house, and I was sorry that he would not let me put my question at that point because he was just then explaining that the theatre owner had the choice of whether to pass this tax on to only a certain class of his theatre patrons, or whether any of the tax should be passed on to his patrons, or whether the tax should be passed on in varying proportions among the theatre patrons. The minister, however, must admit this, that in view of the representations made to him and the Department of Finance with regard to this tax, he held up its application until such time as the theatre owners could make arrangements to pass the tax on to the theatre patrons, and the result is that the theatre owners are going to pass the tax on to their individual patrons. The minister may have considered that so many millions of dollars were being spent in moving-picture theatres by the people of this country that not only was the moving-picture business prosperous but that the people were spending so much money on picture shows, wasting their earnings, that he should levy a tax to curtail such expenditures. Either the tax must come from the theatre owner or be passed on by him to the public. If the minister's idea was to curtail expenditures by the public, goodness knows he is taking enough out of the low income groups already!
With the extension of this tax to other amusements which were not, prior to this amendment, subject to any amusement tax,
I think the minister might very well consider reducing the tax to ten per cent. There is 
no reason at all to believe that he would not receive the same amount of money that he would have received by taxing motion-picture theatres alone the twenty per cent. If he makes that reduction, he will better the financial position of this countiy. At the same time he must consider that those who pay large fees to see the more expensive sports will be let off lightly in comparison with those who patronize the motion-picture theatres, and that is not fair. The minister should carefully consider reducing the tax fifty per cent and making it a ten per cent general amusement tax across the country, so relieving the people who attend the twenty-five cent motion-picture threatres.

I agree with the
previous speaker that, in view of the amendment which was introduced, and is timely, the minister might consider reducing the tax on motion-picture theatres. It is stated that, according to government records, seventy-seven per cent of those who attend motion-picture theatres in Canada pay twenty-five cents admission fee or less. It is my opinion that the motion-picture theatre people render a service, both educational and recreational, to their patrons. What the present proposal will mean in Manitoba is that those theatres which now operate on a twenty-five cent admission fee will have to make an advance of forty per cent. The great majority of the motion-picture theatres in rural Manitoba have an admission charge of twenty-five cents. There is a provincial amusement tax, on tickets over twenty-five cents and under thirty-three cents, of two cents; over that amount, three cents and up. That will mean, with the twenty per cent federal tax on the price of admission, plus the provincial amusement tax, that people will have to pay at least thirty-five cents where formerly they paid twenty-five cents; that is an increase of forty per cent on the price of admission. I repeat that the minister might very well reduce the amount from twenty per cent to ten per cent, in view of the amendment he has introduced this evening to tax certain other amusements throughout the dominion. I do not know what amusements that is intended to include, and I should like to ask the minister one or two questions on the subject.
I am convinced that the proposed additional tax on motion-picture tickets, particularly in theatres operating in rural districts which have not benefited at all by war industries, will reduce attendance at those theatres to a far greater extent than an increase in the tax on liquor would reduce the consumption of liquor at this time.
Under the amendment, will this taxation cover pool-rooms?

No. I do not know just
how a pool-room is run.
I do not know much about it myself, Mr. Chairman.

No.
You pay to get out.
This amendment will only cover admission charges to spectators at, say, a hockey match, or a ball game?

Or bull-fights.

speechtext: It must be an amusement. There is a power of exemption in certain instances.
There would not be a tax on admission fees to exhibitions for recreational purposes, such as athletic competitions of any sort?

speechtext:
If the person intends to
participate; if he is paying to go in to play himself, or to dance; if it is his activity, the tax does not apply.
There will be no tax? Mr. ILSLEY: No.
How does the minister propose to collect from night clubs that put on floor shows? They do not charge admission. They get their fees from a cover charge and extra prices for beer and wines.

speechtext: The tax does not apply to them.
