My chief objection to this tax is an objection which is applicable to all taxes of this kind: it is not a tax on income, and consequently it is not equitable.
I did not rise, however, for the particular purpose of attacking the tax. I have had a number of protests, as most hon. members have had. I believe the objection on the part of the theatre people was that it was not equitable because it did not apply to other amusements. The amendment removes that inequality so far as the theatres are concerned.
I am not greatly concerned with the tax, because I do not believe the condition of the working class can be improved by a ten per cent reduction in the tax on movies. I do not believe it is the high tax on movies which makes the working class poor. The working class is poor because it is exploited, because people who do not work take the value of the
workers' labour; and there is no way in which the working class can be benefited unless we enable them to take the social value of their labour. Therefore I am not going to engage in any hysterics about improving the lot of the working class by providing cheaper beer or cutting ten per cent off the tax on motion-picture shows.
I understand that motion-picture shows for Red Cross purposes are exempt from taxation; but if the man who operates the film receives a fee, is the tax applicable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The entire proceeds must go for charitable, religious or patriotic purposes.
The entire proceeds?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

No
allowance can be made for the man who is putting on the show? Supposing he were paid $10 for exhibiting amateur motion pictures, or 16 mm. motion pictures, on behalf of the Red Cross-perhaps he had travelled ten or fifteen miles for the purpose-would the tax apply?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not say that reasonable expenses might not be allowed. That would be a matter of administration. It might be a reasonable thing to make an allowance. That would seem to be a little different from putting on a performance for profit.

That is what I had in mind, also that the society might have to pay a few dollars for the rental of a hall. The wording of this resolution is, "admission price to a moving picture theatre". That, of course, would cover everything. Suppose the theatre were rented by the Red Cross; would they have to pay the tax? According to this, they would.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am proposing an amendment authorizing the minister to make an exemption where the entire proceeds are for charitable, religious or patriotic purposes. It is not in the resolution as printed, but it will be in the bill.

The
minister also said that there has been an increase in attendances at motion-picture theatres. I went to a motion-picture theatre last night which was not a quarter filled. This was the only Wednesday night when the theatre had not been filled. May I say, also, that it was a really good show, one of the best I have seen. I suggest, therefore, in view
Special War Revenue Act

of the fact that other amusements have been brought under the tax, that the tax on motion-pictures be reduced to ten per cent.

Did I understand the minister to say that no arrangement could be made for the exemption of soldiers? I have in mind one particular camp area. It is the only form of amusement for these men, and I was wondering whether they could be exempted. Would the tax have to be absorbed by the owner of the picture show?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

I assume that even
before the minister brought down the original resolution, he gave the whole subject mature consideration. Is it his opinion that as a result of this amendment he will double the amount of money he expected to receive originally? I see possibilities of that happening. All summer sports will be taxed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no estimate, but I should be very much surprised if the tax doubled the amount to be received, or if it went anywhere near that mark. I may, however, be wrong. There will be many exemptions, and one cannot make an estimate. I think that the field outside motion-picture theatres is, generally speaking, so irregular and so small compared with the main amusement industry of the country that it would be surprising if any result such as is suggested were realized.

I have made a slight calculation, going over in my mind the number of moving-picture shows in my particular area, and I have also taken into consideration arenas and other forms of amusement which are definitely in existence in that district. I am fairly familiar with the admission tickets bought in the other types of amusement, such as arenas, and I still suggest to the minister that if he would post someone to make a careful investigation he would find that my calculation is correct, particularly in the larger areas. If he had some qualified person make a survey of the situation, he would find that 90 per cent of the people in the lower bracket incomes are affected. I concur in the statements that have been made here. I believe that in broadening the field of application of the amusement tax, with which I am in accord, consideration might be given to a reduction so that it would not fall so heavily on the middle-class people, as they are sometimes termed, and on low bracket income people, as we know them in our urban and larger centres. I urge that because I am quite 
certain the minister will find that the field he has opened up will yield double the amount he expected to receive from the tax.

I have had letters and telegrams of protest, but no invitations to have further taxes imposed on other forms of entertainment, because where I come from we have now more taxes than we can pay and we are not asking for any more. The conditions under which theatre operators in my part of the country carry on are entirely different from those cited by hon. gentlemen who have already spoken. In a good many instances, the theatres cited are operated six days and nights a week, but in my own case some operators cover as many as five or six towns; and because a number of men have enlisted from those towns, the theatre operators are having to cut out some of the towns altogether. It has been suggested that in some districts 150 or more men have enlisted. It has been the practice of a number of these men to take their lady friends to the pictures; but now that the men have gone, the girls have not the salaries, which are small even here, to enable them to attend the moving pictures, and they must stay at home. That works a hardship on the motion-picture operators there.
I do not know whether there is any use in protesting against the tax, because we know what happened in connection with the gasoline tax. This one, while not as unjust, does not apply in the places in which it should. Here in the city of Ottawa the civil servants get $60 a month to start with, and those in employment for more than six months have been given a boost of $5 a month. First, they have been accustomed to the lower national defence tax, and now it is five per cent, so that I do not know whether we are in a much worse position out there than here, because, while the government causes a little bit of money to be given to people, they find some means of deducting it, and the deductions are, in many instances, far greater than the amount given.

I believe there will be general approval of the amendment brought in by the minister. There is a feeling that if the government must raise revenue by taxing amusements, it should not tax just one branch and let other branches go scot-free. Personally, I think it is unfortunate to have to tax amusements, because they are a large factor in building up public morale; but the government must find revenue, and if they are going to tax amusements, the tax should apply to all. In spite of what the minister

Special War Revenue Act
says, the fact remains that people in the low income brackets do use the motion pictures almost exclusively as their sole form of recreation. I like to go to prize fights; but why should I pay seventy-five cents to see a prize fight and not pay a tax, while others pay twenty-five cents to see a moving picture and pay a tax? The minister's amendment will meet with approval, and if he finds that he must tax amusements he should apply it to all forms.
I agree with him that there should be certain exemptions, but I am wondering how he is going to take care of them. Probably there will be some details in the bill; but it seems to me that if an application must be made to the Minister of National Revenue every time a group of people wish to put on an entertainment, there will be a great many difficulties. Many of these entertainments are got up in a hurry, and in many of the rural areas the ladies who put them on know little or nothing about the tax. Throughout my constituency in the country places the ladies of the Red Cross and of other organizations get together and put on a social in a few days. Are they liable to prosecution if they do not charge the tax? I am offering a suggestion to the minister. Would it be possible in the bill to make a blanket exception for certain classes of entertainment put on for charitable, religious and patriotic purposes? Second, would it be possible to give the minister power to declare exemption in special cases? As I understood him, any group of people putting on an entertainment will have to make application, provided they come in one of the three categories mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is what is proposed.

Would the
tax be easier to administer if the minister said that all entertainments put on for the purpose of raising money for charitable, religious or patriotic purposes are exempt, -without making application, and that in cases which do not come under those three classifications they must apply to the minister? I realize there will be many border-line cases, -and the minister will have to have wide discretionary power. I realize that there is not a blanket clause to cover all these small fraternal and patriotic societies and charitable institutions. There will be scores of entertainments put on as to which either the people putting them on will not have to make application or they will not know of the tax. The minister will have endless confusion. Would he give some consideration to my suggestion?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, I will give consideration to that suggestion. I may say that my first thought was to do just that, to make a statutory exemption of amusements the whole proceeds of which were to go to a charitable or religious purpose, and give the minister discretion in the other classes. But this gives the department greater control, and there may be instances where opinions will differ widely as to what purposes are charitable, or patriotic, or perhaps even religious. I do not know. There is so much scope for difference of opinion regarding this that it would make for more thorough administration to require application in all instances.

How long in
advance would an organization have to make application in order to secure a permit?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is a matter of detail
which would have to be worked out. The national revenue department has an extensive organization all across Canada, and it may be that there could be quite a degree of decentralization.

I am not sure that this
question is quite fair in so far as the exceptions introduced by the minister cannot be fully comprehended at this moment while the discussion is going on. I asked him as to the position of fall fairs, for instance. I do not see that they can be included under the classification of exemptions enunciated by him as being charitable, patriotic or religious. There is a broad field that might be called educational which would be equally entitled to exemption. There are church socials, garden parties which might be held by social, fraternal or even economic societies, on which a tax of twenty per cent would be extremely onerous.
I suggest with all deference that the resolution might be framed a little more clearly, and that hon. members should have a copy before them before they are asked to pass it even in the committee stage, because I believe many complications could arise with the resolution in its present form. Hon. members should have a definite, clear-cut resolution and time to consider it before discussion is ended. The discussion so far amply illustrates that point. It is difficult for hon. members to delve into the realm of imagination and conjure up all the circumstances that might arise under this tax. The difficulty is that the tax is twenty per cent. There is even a problem whether a religious, patriotic or charitable society might put on some form of entertainment on a profit-sharing basis. That also should be considered. It is not every society that could put on an entertainment to raise
Special War Revenue Act

money for charitable, religious or patriotic purposes that could produce the entertainment without paying something to the personnel engaged in putting it on. I believe much time would be gained if the discussion of this resolution were deferred until a more clear-cut proposal is before the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The resolution commits the committee to just two things: first, that a like tax of twenty per cent be imposed on certain other forms of amusement. I take it that all members of the committee are in favour of that; all who have spoken are. I think; second, that the said tax is to come into effect on a date to be proclaimed by the governor in council. It is not the place of the committee to settle the exact terms of an enactment. The bill is always, or practically always, much longer and more detailed and exact than the resolution. This resolution is to give notice, to settle the principle, and to give hon. members time to gather themselves together and criticize the bill when it comes down. I do not think the committee should ask that the resolution be held up for the reason stated by the hon. member.
To the question of fairs I have given some thought. I do not think there will be much difficulty in working it out. The speeches that have been made show why we were diffident in entering this other field of amusement, because hon. members could speak for days about it; some would have in mind certain things that must be let off, and more and more they would think of other things that must be let off. Yet, theoretically and in general, they would urge that the whole field of amusement be covered. Those are two conflicting points of view that the government has to struggle with in this matter. I ask hon. members to be a little tolerant about this. We cannot just tax something that is far away and does not hurt us; we must have rules, and the rules will get close to us once in a while.
Is it clearly understood that admissions to agricultural exhibitions, county exhibitions, are excluded from this tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot make any commitment about a particular exhibition. There might, I suppose, be a profit-making fair.

I refer to agricultural exhibitions such as are held all over Canada, certainly in Nova Scotia and in my own constituency, annual exhibitions carried on by agricultural societies, farmers' clubs and such organizations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would think there is power to exempt them under what I have proposed.
What would be the process for such an exhibition to ascertain whether they get the exemption? Will there be some local authority, or would that application have to be made to the minister at Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would expect it would be made to the local collector of customs. The national revenue department has an organization all across the country, and usually applications can be made to the nearest or any collector of customs.

It should be understood that such agricultural exhibitions would be exempt from this tax.
Would the minister not consider an amendment which would exempt from this tax theatre tickets for children, and matinee admissions? I think it is recognized that these low-priced tickets should not be subject to a tax if that can be avoided ; and I should think this could be done in view of the fact that the proposed amendments will greatly increase the revenue accruing to the department in comparison with what was contemplated when the minister brought down the budget. If the minister could give such an undertaking, it would meet with approval in this house and throughout the country, particularly on the part of those having large families and those who are able to attend only the less expensive theatre performances.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know whether the hon. gentleman was in the chamber at that time, but that matter was discussed. I pointed out that this was an indirect tax on the proprietors of these places of amusement. It is not upon the people who attend. The proprietors may pass on the tax, or they may not. Of course they will pass it on, but they can pass it on in such proportions as they wish, and to whomever they wish. It would be meaningless to insert an exception of that kind; and moreover I would not be in favour of it. I am not in favour of relaxing or modifying that twenty per cent. I have seen scores-I was going to say hundreds-of telegrams which have been received by members of parliament from operators of theatres all over the country. Most of these telegrams take no exception to the tax or to the amount of the tax. I can well understand that hon. members might say they do not care what the motion-picture people think; that they desire to urge a lower tax in the interests of the patrons of [DOT] the moving-picture theatres. This is a heavy tax: it is designed to be such. It is said that it will injure the morale of

Special War Revenue Act
this country; but the need of maintaining morale is not so obvious here as it is in Great Britain. What I sense in a great many parts of Canada is just a little bit of the boom spirit, which is not the kind of morale we want at all.

It seems to me that a rebate such as I suggest could be administered very easily on the basis of the number of low-priced tickets sold by the theatre operator, if the minister would agree to that principle. This is a heavy tax for central Canada, but, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Souris, it is an especially serious tax in that province and also in Nova Scotia. In my province we have a provincial tax as well, and with this dominion tax the rates paid in Nova Scotia will be:

This double taxation violates the principle that has been laid down, namely, that there should be uniformity of taxation. Of course, part of the revenue accrues to the province; but, as I said this afternoon in connection with the gasoline tax, Nova Scotia imposes a tax on theatre admissions and a heavier tax on gasoline, but does not impose an income tax. The income tax is levelled up by means of rebates to compensate provinces for what they may lose by only the federal tax being imposed. Nova Scotia and New Brunswick do not impose provincial income taxes, so they will get no provincial rebates, but they pay proportionately heavier taxes as a result of this budget. This violates the principle of equality of taxation, because this theatre tax is a double tax in Nova Scotia, I should like to see a rebate allowed on cheaper tickets, tickets to children. The minister has, however, stated his opposition to any such rebates, and therefore I suppose we must accept his ruling.

I have listened patiently to this discussion this evening, and I intend to take only about one minute to make a few observations. The minister has seen fit to amend this resolution, and I think his amendment will meet with the approval of all hon. members. I only wish he might have been convinced so easily with respect to the gasoline tax. Like many other hon. members, I have received a great many telegrams from theatre operators in the west, particularly in my own neighbourhood. One telegram has come from a man who operates five theatres, and another from a man who operates four. This is a popular, cheap form of amusement
in the rural parts of western Canada, where the farmers come to town on Friday or Saturday night. Most of the theatres in the rural sections of the west are operated only two nights a week, on Friday and Saturday; and if the minister could see the number of people who gather at these shows on those evenings, I think he would be convinced that this is a real source of amusement for the western people. The protests contained in the telegrams I received were to the effect that twenty per cent of the gross receipts was too much; they thought it should be reduced to something like ten per cent. That was the opinion of the man who operates the five theatres.
I do not think I need labour the point further. I hope the minister will take that suggestion into consideration and reduce the tax to ten per cent, at least in connection with those theatres operating in the rural sections. I presume any reduction would have to apply to all theatres, but it is in the rural sections that it would be most appreciated.

I should like to urge upon the minister that in working out these amendments he keep in mind the fact that agricultural fairs are not profit-making organizations. In the past, certain classes of fairs have received federal grants; others have received provincial grants; and still others, municipal grants. If these fairs were taxed in any way, I believe many would cease to operate. It is true that admissions are charged, and that the fairs are partly educational and partly entertaining; but at the same time they render a service to the community. Therefore I hope the minister will keep this point in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Why is there not a tax on night clubs putting on floor shows? I am afraid we are going to drive people from the theatres to the night clubs, and I do not think we want them to go there.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no admission charged to night clubs.
They put on entertainment, though.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The difficulty of administration would be very great there.

There is a
cover charge, is there not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Sometimes there is a cover charge, and in some clubs there is a cover charge on certain nights and not on others
Special War Revenue Act

They have all sorts of ways of making money, but I think their chief revenue comes from the sale of beer and food. I think those are the main sources of revenue in night clubs.
That is where the people are spending their money to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are taxing them on the gasoline that they use to get there; we are taxing them on the beer that they drink when they are there, and we are taxing them on several other things. There is no admission charge upon which we can tax them, and we did not think we could go into that.
Mr. O'BRIEN: Could that tax not be imposed on the same basis as the hospital tax in Quebec?

I have just come from
another committee, and therefore I am not familiar with the discussion that has taken place. I take it that the main object of this tax is to conserve foreign exchange. Could some exemption not be granted in so far as British films are concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The question of exchange has not been mentioned as yet in the discussion, and that is not the main object of this tax. I am doubtful whether any foreign exchange will be saved because the films will come in just the same whether or not the people are taxed.

How long will this tax be in
effect?
Mr. ILSLEY': I do not know about that.
Will it cease with the end of the war or before?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I cannot say.
Mr. O'BRIEN: I asked the minister whether the tax on night clubs could not be collected in the same way as the hospital tax in Quebec, but he did not give me an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are fields into which we could go if we went to enough trouble. I do not know how the hospital tax in Quebec is collected, but I have the impression that one pays a cent or two on meals, or something like that. We do not intend to do that. It certainly is a wonderful experience to have hon. members urging us into more fields of taxation, but I am afraid that once we got it established, the applications for exemptions vould be tremendous.

10.	That there shall be imposed, levied and collected an excise tax of five per cent of the total amount of bets made through the agency of a pari mutuel system on any horse race run at a lawful meeting, such tax to be payable by the person conducting the race meeting.

What will this tax
bring in?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: About 81,000,000 in a full year.

Should this tax not be increased? No one likes a horse race better than I, but at the same time I think I should be willing to pay at least ten per cent when I bet money on a horse race. We are taxing gasoline which is used for productive purposes, to the extent of 15 per cent; we are taxing moving picture theatres used for educational and recreational purposes, to the extent of twenty per cent, and I cannot see why horse racing, which certainly is not essential, should not have a higher tax imposed on it. This is not a poor man's game, and I think there should be parity of taxation. I would suggest increasing this tax to ten per cent and reducing some of the other taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are not the only ones in the field here; the provinces are in it as well. It must always be borne in mind that we cannot crowd the provinces out of all these fields of taxation. Hon. gentlemen are continually talking as though we were the only taxing authority. We are branching out when we go into this amusement field. I have not the slightest desire to be unfair to the provinces. It is a matter of judgment as to how high this particular tax should be. It must be remembered that there is a provincial tax as well as a charge on the betting for the benefit of the owners of the track. I think, in the interests of revenue, we have gone about as high as we should.
I would remind the minister that the provinces also tax gasoline and moving-picture theatres.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is no argument for taxing everything else.

I grant the minister that, but he has taxed the poor people on something which is essential to the life of this country to a much greater degree than horse racing. He has gone into the provincial field in those instances.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are on sugar.

As the committee will
readily see, this resolution provides for a tax to be placed upon com syrup. The St. Lawrence Starch company, perhaps the largest producer of corn syrup in Canada, is located in Port Credit in my constituency.
I understand that up to now there has been no tax on corn syrup when sold in packages containing not more than ten pounds each.
I believe I am reliably informed when I say to the minister that this tax will interfere severely with the business now carried on at that point.
In addition to the possibility of restricting the sales of this commodity, there is another angle to this matter which I desire to stress at this time. Corn syrup is a commodity used largely by our working people and ' farmers, it is used by the man in the lower income brackets. When a tax is added upon
Special War Revenue Act

com syrup in less than ten pound quantities, the government immediately enters into that field, to the detriment of people with very low incomes. I have spoken to the minister privately about this, but I would appeal to him now to consider further this proposal of placing a tax of two cents upon tins of corn syrup less than ten pounds in weight.
There is another angle affecting another branch of our primary production. Since February, 1941, this plant has processed no less than 200,000 bushels of Ontario grown corn. That radically affects several people, particularly in Essex East and other ridings which are well known for their excellent corn products, and I hope that I shall be able to get some measure of support from hon. members representing those constituencies. In the past, while corn from Africa and the United States has been used, the starch companies are ever anxious to use more Canadian grown corn, and I think the minister will admit that 200,000 bushels of com processed since February of this year is by no means a small quantity. If this tax has the effect, as I am reliably informed it will have, of restricting the consumption of corn syrup, that is going to affect not only the working classes of our country and the farmers who consume this product but growers of corn throughout Ontario, upon whom it will work a hardship.
I should also like to stress another point, namely, that there is discrimination in this tax, which is perhaps one of the worst features of it. Molasses, which is a competitive product with corn syrup, is not taxed, and some other commodities which enter into direct competition with com syrup bear no tax at all. It does seem to me-and I would bring this as sharply to the minister's attention as I possibly can-that if we are not going to tax a wide range of similar commodities, it is not fair or equitable to tax one particular commodity only and leave competitive commodities tax free. That is a principle which should not be adopted by the government even in war time, and I ask the minister whether he will not, in all fairness, restore the conditions which existed so far as this product is concerned before the budget was brought down.

I am sure that the invitation of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Graydon) is one which I as member for Essex county in the corn belt of Canada could not very well overlook.
Before supporting him in the representations he has made to-night. I am certain that I express the views of all members of this house when I offer him sincere congratulations upon the appointment which was accorded

him this morning. I sincerely trust that, as a result of his organizing ability, his party will always remain in second place in the political life of this country.
The corn belt of Canada is situated in the southwestern peninsula of this province. Some five counties are vitally concerned. In the county of Essex and the county of Kent sixty-five per cent of the corn of Canada is grown, and in southwestern Ontario, eighty-five per cent of the corn of Canada is grown. Therefore the farmers of that area, growing corn as a cash crop, are naturally very much interested in an opportunity of increasing their acreage and, consequently, their income.
While the starch company to which the hon. gentleman has referred does not purchase as much corn from western Ontario as it might, nevertheless there is a potential market there, and one which this government, made fully aware of the facts, would, I am certain, wish to encourage. Therefore I cannot help but support the observations of the hon. gentleman.
Honey, molasses, corn syrup-these are things that are found on the table of the masses of the people, and there should be no discrimination in respect to any one of these commodities so far as the tax is concerned, but as the resolution now stands, corn syrup is singled out. It should not be placed in that singular position; it should not be discriminated against, giving other commodities competing with it an advantage. I propose, when the agriculture estimates come up, to discuss this question more fully, but at the moment I strongly support the observations of the hon. member for Peel.
If the hon. member would permit a question, does he intend to discuss the agriculture estimates from a legal point of view or from a farmer's point of view?
I hope to discuss them from a sensible point of view.

The people of my district feel a deep debt of gratitude towards this product of corn syrup. Notwithstanding that, however, I consider I am representing their views by, in the public interest, not opposing this additional impost.
The minister should, I think, outline the position of the government. He has not made any reply to my protests.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The question of whether corn syrup should be taxed has been under consideration for a good many years. It is very hard to draw the line in such a way between these food products as not to give rise to the charge of discrimination by the

Special War Revenue Act
manufacturers of some particular food product. The manufacturers who have had a grievance for many years past have been the jam manufacturers, who have claimed that corn syrup is in competition with jam, and that the jam manufacturers have been subject to the sugar tax, which now is a two cents a pound tax, and that this gives the corn syrup manufacturers an undue and unfair advantage, and the jam manufacturers charge discrimination.
It is true that we are drawing a line between molasses and corn syrup instead of between corn syrup and jam. Naturally, the corn syrup manufacturers immediately enter very, very strong protests and say that they are now the aggrieved parties. We did not extend the tax to molasses because there we are getting into a product a large part of which is used for stock-feeding purposes and a small part for human consumption.
They are two entirely different products.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed that it would be difficult to draw a distinction for administrative purposes. At any rate, there is something to be said for the contention that molasses is more of a poor man's food than corn syrup.
Both are consumed by the poorer classes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not sure about that, but it sounds that way to me, at any rate.
It doesn't taste that way.

May I suggest to the minister that his comparison with the tax which is put on jams is not a parallel case at all, because jams do not consist wholly of sugar, and a two-cent tax on the sugar in the jam is only a tax on a portion of the entire product. When the minister places a two-cent tax on corn syrup, he taxes the whole value of the product; that is not the situation with a two-cent tax on whatever sugar is contained in the jam. It may seem that this is a rather pointed suggestion ; but I submit to the minister that it is a discriminatory tax, and I know that, if he is convinced' of that, he would be the last one to insist upon imposing it. I wish to impress upon him the necessity of avoiding the process of destroying one competitor and setting up another. That is a principle which I do not believe for a moment the government would consider. I hope that between the present time and when the amendment is brought down, he will give this matter some further consideration, and will realize just what he is proposing to do to the corn syrup manufacturers of Canada. I
really believe that here is a serious discrimination. The outcry from these companies, as the minister knows, is very strong. They fear that the proposed tax will prejudicially affect their business, and put their competitors in a position in which they should not be put, at least by government action.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What is the competition they fear? Molasses?

The competition of
molasses is, I am informed, important, especially in the province of Quebec.

speechtext:
Resolution agreed to.
18.	That the tax on carbonic acid gas and similar preparations used for aerating nonalcoholic beverages provided for in section four of schedule II to the said act be increased from five cents per pound to twenty-five cents per pound.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have to propose an amendment. This tax, as it stands in the resolution, does not satisfy me and has not satisfied me from the beginning. In the first place, it seems to me far too light, when one considers that the amount of money paid for soft drinks in Canada is something like $55,000,000 a year. One sees every day in the streets these large trucks loaded with soft drinks, especially, of course, during the summer months, and in my opinion it is a legitimate object of taxation. The industry itself does not deny this.
In the past we imposed the tax on the carbonic acid gas. That has had certain disadvantages. In the first place, still drinks, so-called, are competitive with the aerated beverages, and it seems unfair to place a tax on the aerated beverages without imposing any on still drinks.
That is the same principle as I raised before.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
With regard to corn syrup? Well, yes; but in that other field I do not know where you will move the line, unless you take it off everything, not to have some demarcation; and in this instance, when the tax on the aerated beverages becomes substantial, a discrimination between them and the still drinks exists which should not be there. There is some advantage in a tax on carbonic acid gas, in that it taxes the counter drinks, which some other forms of tax would not do.
Therefore, everything having been taken into account, it has been decided to propose this amendment. It puts a very much heavier tax on the soft drink industry, but it also eliminates a great deal of discrimination. In the representations which have been made tc
Special War Revenue Act

the officials of the department and to myself, the stress has been laid on the undesirability of discrimination rather than on the undesirability of taxation. The proposed carbonic acid gas tax resulted, I will not say in frenzied protests, but certainly in strenuous and repeated protests, delegations, petitions, all sorts of communications by telegram, letter and otherwise, and I think there is considerable ground for them. I am not sure that what I am going to propose will suit the industry any better, but it is going to be a much fairer tax and a much heavier tax. The amendment, which is an addition to resolution 18, reads:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend resolution No. 18, proposing amendments to the Special War Revenue Act introduced on April twenty-ninth, one thousand nine hundred and forty-one by adding thereto the following: "That schedule I to the said act be amended by adding thereto the following section as section eight:
_ 8. Beverages consisting of unfermented fruit juices and imitations thereof; carbonated beverages or aerated waters; all other compounded or mixed soft drinks put up in bottles for sale-25 per cent and to provide for exemption from the tax on carbonic acid gas in cases where this commodity is used in the manufacture of the said beverages."
That any enactment founded on this resolution shall be deemed to have come into force on the twenty-third day of May, nineteen hundred and forty-one.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I so move.
It is twenty-five per cent of what?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will be twenty-five per cent of the sale price by the manufacturer.
This will not apply to apple juice?
How much was it proposed to raise under No. 18 as it originally stood, and how much will the estimated revenue be under the resolution as amended?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The estimate under the tax as originally proposed, for the full year, was $2,000,000, but I am told that is high and that it would probably not have yielded that much. An estimate of the amount to be obtained under the resolution as amended would be $6,000,000 or $7,000,000.

I do not quite follow
this as it is now before the committee. If I understand it aright, the resolution as amended is what appears in resolution 18, and we add this amendment to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is correct.
(Mr. Ilsley.]
In that event, it appears to me that resolution 18 imposes a tax on carbonic acid gas and the second paragraph of the amendment exempts it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Only when it is used in the
manufacture of the drinks which are subject to the twenty-five per cent ad valorem tax.

That is what resolution
18 says-"used for aerating non-alcoholic beverages."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, but there is the soda
fountain business. Under this proposal the carbonic acid gas tax will apply on the sale of carbonic acid gas to proprietors of soda fountains. There will be no way of escaping that. But if it is sold to manufacturers of drinks, that is, bottlers who manufacture drinks and put them up in bottles, then they buy it tax free, and the twenty-five per cent tax steps in on the sale price of that manufactured product.

20. That the said schedule III be further amended by deleting therefrom the items under the caption "building materials".

With regard to resolution 20, I have been asked to make certain representations. There is a great shortage of houses in the city of Brantford, more particularly working men's houses.
I hold in my hand a copy of the Brantford Expositor of Tuesday May 13, in which there appears an article on the front page under the heading "Housing problem again discussed by council". The housing problem there, being as severe as it is, has been discussed in the city council on many occasions. To-day there are not sufficient houses in the city to house the working people, and the city council had arranged for the building of low cost houses. It was proposed to build these houses under the National Housing Act. It will be recalled that under that act, where the total cost of the house including land is $2,500, the lending company and the government will advance up to ninety per cent of the cost. When the city was making arrangements to build these low cost houses, the eight per cent tax on building materials was not in existence. With the addition of the eight per cent tax on building materials it is absolutely impossible to build a working man's house for $2,500. It puts it beyond the $2,500 class. I may be asked, why not pay the additional money, which is $2,600 or $2,700? My answer is that when you get beyond the $2,500 class you do not get the ninety per cent of the cost of building as a loan; you are limited to eighty per cent.
I also hold in my hand a resolution passed by the council of the city of Brantford in which they refer to the scarcity of houses for rental purposes. The resolution refers to the additional tax on building materials and is to this effect. In the first place, the city requests that the eight per cent tax shall not apply on building materials which go into the construction of low-cost homes. Whether that can be worked out and whether the act could be administered in such a way that the tax would not affect low cost homes, I cannot say, but I know that rebates have been given by the department in other connections. In the second place, the resolution requests that the loan on low-cost houses should apply to any house costing $3,000 or less. The increase in the cost of building is not only in connection with the eight per
cent additional tax but also in connection with other costs which have gone up. When the National Housing Act was brought down, I thought it was quite proper to have the ninety per cent loan applied only to houses costing $2,500, but to-day a working man's house cannot be built for $2,500; the minimum is $3,000. The housing act is administered by the Minister of Finance, and I would respectfully suggest to him that if it is impossible to take off the eight per cent on building materials which go into low-cost houses, he step up the amount from $2,500 to $3,000 so that ninety per cent loans can be applied to that class of houses.
I wish to take this opportunity to congratulate the Minister of Finance not only upon his address of several weeks ago, when he presented the budget, but also upon his patience and the courteous manner in which he has presented these resolutions to the committee. I know we all appreciate it very much. I am sure he will take into careful consideration my suggestion on behalf of the working people of Brantford that some provision be made whereby we can build workingmen's houses.
Houses for the workingmen of every town and city.

I endorse what has been said by the hon. member for Brantford City. On Wednesday May 7 I discussed the question of war-time housing, making special reference to this item. On that occasion I discussed the matter from the point of view of our war industries, pointing out that at the beginning of the last war we had a surplus of from 7 to 15 per cent of vacant houses in Canada as a whole, whereas at the present time we have a surplus of possibly around one per cent. Since I delivered my speech on May 7, I have had communications from many places, from British Columbia, Alberta and Manitoba, stating that in the larger centres where there are war industries and military encampments there is a serious shortage of housing. I was told of one place in British Columbia where twenty-five people are living in one house in which there is just one bathroom. We have a serious problem of overcrowding in nearly all the cities in Canada, especially those in which there are war industries.	*
The minister, in his budget speech, in discussing this question mentioned having refrained during nearly two years of war from suggesting any discouragement to building. He said:
Having refrained during nearly two years of war from suggesting any discouragement to building, it has now been decided to recommend the removal of building materials from the list
308S
Special War Revenue Act

of exemptions under the sales tax. In the meantime, the provision for home improvement loans has been exhausted, the application of the National Housing Act has been narrowed, and the War-time Housing Corporation has been set up to provide for the more urgent housing needs.
On that occasion I pointed out that the appropriation for war-time housing was altogether too small in view of the urgency of the problem. We are embarking upon an expenditure of around a billion dollars a year, and the experience in the United States during the last war indicates that there might very well be a wastage of ten per cent as a result of our not having adequate housing. At the present time we have a surplus of labour in many communities, but as more men enter the army and greater difficulty is experienced in securing housing, these war industries are going to suffer from men being unable to live near their work and find housing for their families.
I think the minister has not given this problem the consideration it deserves. Would he be good enough to make a statement at this time as to the findings of his department in connection with the housing problem in Canada, and as to whether the representations that I am sure have been made to him regarding the removal of building materials from the sales tax exemption is not going to have an injurious effect on the efforts to cope with this urgent problem? As the hon. member for Brantford City has pointed out, I believe we are going to have great difficulty in getting low-priced housing built under the national housing scheme in a great many of these cities where there is great need. Would the minister be kind enough to make a statement now or to-morrow regarding the housing problem as it is viewed by his department?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not in a position to make any extended statement; it is five minutes to eleven anyway. The reason why this exemption is being removed is this. Building materials were subject to sales tax until three or four years ago when they were exempted to meet a specific situation. It was one of the steps taken to relieve unemployment. That is now ended; we have not an unemployment situation in the country, quite the contrary.
But we are short of housing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The reason why building materials were removed from the sales tax exemption no longer exists. I should not think there would be any notable break in the building of housing as a result of making 
these materials again subject to sales tax. A great deal of the need for housing is for housing of the type handled by the War-time Housing Corporation, not the type which goes on under the National Housing Act. The housing corporation is doing it on behalf of the government; the government is owning the houses, and this private building will, I think, go on under present conditions pretty rapidly and successfully whether this tax is on or not.
The tax is a means of obtaining revenue,, an important revenue item, the amount expected to be derived from the tax being $15,000,000 for a full year.
The main representations that I have had recently from the construction industry have-not been in reference to the proposed step; they have been in reference to the necessity of obtaining licences for non-residential building.

The minister has said that this tax will not affect building. Here is a letter I have received from the city clerk at Peterborough. He says:
I may say that a number of people have been in the last six weeks interested in city lots for the purpose of erecting homes but since the sales tax announcement their plans have been shelved. ^Unless some action is taken in the sales tax it is quite definitely apparent that the building of homes in this district will be-limited this year.
I understand that the National Housing Act has been fixed so as to take care of this sales tax; the valuation has been advanced.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Has it?

I
understand so from the housing department. But the advance is so much that these people cannot afford it, especially on top of the national defence tax, which is going to raise the price of labour, and that also will have to be taken into consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman, what are these persons in his constituency who have changed their plans, going to do instead for shelter?
Most of them are people in key-positions in war industry. They will have to stay on, perhaps two or three families in a house, which they do not want to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not the policy of the government to encourage people to build unnecessarily. The policy is to divert as much as possible of the labour and material resources of the nation into the war effort,

Foreign-Language Newspapers
rather than into the building of houses for themselves if that can be deferred. We are looking at things differently now from the way we were in 1937 and 1938, in just the opposite way. Then we had unemployment, and it was desirable to get as many people to build houses for themselves as possible. Now it is desirable for them to make the old house do as far as they possibly can, so as to leave the steel for the radiators free-if it is steel.
Iron.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The iron and all the materials that go into building. Instead of this nation devoting its efforts to the satisfaction of private demands, civilian demands, we want to make those efforts available as much as possible for the prosecution of the war. That is a sound reason for not continuing in our revenue laws an exception which was made to meet a specific situation three or four years ago.

Yes, but the populations of Brantford and of Peterborough have been continually increasing, and we need new homes. The War-time Housing Corporation is putting up homes, but after the war is over, those homes will be tom down and perhaps given away, at a loss of $800 or $900 to the government in connection with each unit. Under this suggestion the government would not lose a cent. I have here a magazine published in the United States which says:
One thing all investigators agree on: The lack of good housing for defence workers is slowing up America's rearmament programme.
Another publication of the Pan-American Union says that in Costa Rica a housing programme is under way. Even there the government is financing the programme itself. I know it is eleven o'clock, Mr. Chairman, but I shall take only a moment to finish. I believe the minister should give some consideration to this proposal. Let the builders pay the tax on building material, but in connection with these low-cost houses there should be a rebate of some kind. Give some encouragement to the man who is working to carry on, raise his family and own his own home. Give him something to work for. The minister will not be doing that if he does not restrict this tax on building material as it has been restricted in the past. It is not fair to the man who is working.
Progress reported.
